questions.question: A chemical or physical process is said to have reached equilibrium when:
options: The forward process has stopped completely
The forward and reverse processes occur at equal rates so that measurable properties stay constant
All the reactants have been converted into products
The reverse process has stopped completely
questions.explanation: Equilibrium in a closed system is dynamic: both the forward and reverse processes continue, but since their rates become equal, the concentrations (or other measurable properties like colour, pressure) stop changing with time. Nothing actually stops.
questions.hint: Think 'dynamic', not 'frozen'.
distractor_logic: Confuses equilibrium with the forward reaction stopping (static view, wrong)
Confuses equilibrium with complete conversion (a very large K, not equilibrium itself)
Confuses equilibrium with the reverse reaction stopping (static view, wrong)

questions.question: For the physical equilibrium H<sub>2</sub>O(l) ↔ H<sub>2</sub>O(g) in a closed vessel at constant temperature, the equilibrium is characterised by:
options: A constant, temperature-dependent vapour pressure above the liquid
Complete evaporation of the liquid over time
No vapour above the liquid at all
A vapour pressure that keeps rising indefinitely
questions.explanation: In a closed vessel the rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation once the vapour pressure reaches a fixed value characteristic of that liquid at that temperature — this is the equilibrium (or saturated) vapour pressure.
questions.hint: What stays constant once a covered cup of water 'stops' evaporating visibly?
distractor_logic: Ignores that the vessel is closed, so vapour cannot escape and build indefinitely
Reverses the correct answer — pressure plateaus, it does not rise forever
Treats it like an open system rather than a closed one

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a solid-liquid physical equilibrium?
options: Water boiling away completely in an open pan
Sugar completely dissolving in hot water
Iodine vapour condensing fully onto a cold surface
Ice and water coexisting at 0°C in an insulated flask
questions.explanation: Ice ↔ Water at 0°C (at 1 atm) is the classic solid-liquid equilibrium: the rate of melting equals the rate of freezing, so the ice-water ratio stays constant if no heat is added or removed.
questions.hint: Look for the option where two phases of the same substance coexist without one being used up.
distractor_logic: Describes total loss of one phase (open system, not equilibrium)
Describes complete dissolution, not an equilibrium of two coexisting phases
Describes a one-way phase change going to completion, not a coexistence

questions.topic: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constant
questions.question: For the general reaction aA + bB ↔ cC + dD, the law of chemical equilibrium states that at a given temperature, K<sub>c</sub> equals:
options: ([C]+[D]) / ([A]+[B]) at equilibrium
[A]<sup>a</sup>[B]<sup>b</sup> / [C]<sup>c</sup>[D]<sup>d</sup> at equilibrium
[C][D] / [A][B], regardless of stoichiometric coefficients
[C]<sup>c</sup>[D]<sup>d</sup> / [A]<sup>a</sup>[B]<sup>b</sup> at equilibrium
questions.explanation: K<sub>c</sub> is the ratio of the product of equilibrium molar concentrations of products to that of reactants, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient in the balanced equation.
questions.hint: Products go on top, reactants on the bottom, coefficients become exponents.
distractor_logic: Uses sums instead of products/powers — not how the law of mass action is written
Inverts the equilibrium constant expression (that would be K for the reverse reaction)
Drops the stoichiometric coefficients as exponents, which changes the expression

questions.topic: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constant
questions.question: The equilibrium constant K<sub>c</sub> for a reaction at a fixed temperature:
options: Is always equal to 1
Is independent of the initial concentrations and has a fixed value at that temperature
Depends on the initial concentrations of reactants taken
Changes if a catalyst is added
questions.explanation: K<sub>c</sub> depends only on temperature for a given reaction. Whatever the starting concentrations, the system settles at equilibrium concentrations that satisfy the same K<sub>c</sub> value.
questions.hint: What is the one variable that changes K?
distractor_logic: K equals 1 only for special reactions — it can range over many orders of magnitude
A very common misconception — the equilibrium position (concentrations) can vary with starting amounts, but K itself does not
Catalysts speed up attainment of equilibrium; they never change the value of K

questions.topic: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constant
questions.question: A very large value of K<sub>c</sub> (say, 10<sup>15</sup>) for a reaction indicates that at equilibrium:
options: The reaction has not started
The reaction mixture is mostly products
Reactants and products are present in exactly equal amounts
The reaction mixture is mostly reactants
questions.explanation: Since K<sub>c</sub> is products over reactants, a very large K<sub>c</sub> means the numerator (products) vastly outweighs the denominator (reactants) at equilibrium — the reaction proceeds nearly to completion.
questions.hint: Products are on top of the K expression.
distractor_logic: A reaction that hasn't started is not at equilibrium at all, and K describes the equilibrium state
Equal amounts would give K close to 1, not 10<sup>15</sup>
Reverses the interpretation of a large K

questions.question: An equilibrium in which all reactants and products are in the same physical phase is called:
options: A dynamic equilibrium only
A heterogeneous equilibrium
A physical equilibrium only
A homogeneous equilibrium
questions.explanation: When every species (e.g. all gases, as in N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 3H<sub>2</sub>(g) ↔ 2NH<sub>3</sub>(g)) is in one phase, the equilibrium is homogeneous. Different phases (e.g. a solid and a gas) make it heterogeneous.
questions.hint: 'Homo' = same.
distractor_logic: 'Dynamic' describes how both forward and reverse processes continue at equal rates — a feature of every equilibrium, not something unique to same-phase (homogeneous) systems
Swaps the meaning of homogeneous and heterogeneous
'Physical' equilibrium refers to a physical (not chemical) change, not to how many phases are involved — a homogeneous equilibrium can be either physical or chemical

questions.question: For the heterogeneous equilibrium CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) ↔ CaO(s) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g), the correct K<sub>c</sub> expression is:
options: K<sub>c</sub> = [CO<sub>2</sub>]
K<sub>c</sub> = [CaO] / [CaCO<sub>3</sub>]
K<sub>c</sub> = [CaCO<sub>3</sub>] / [CaO][CO<sub>2</sub>]
K<sub>c</sub> = [CaO][CO<sub>2</sub>] / [CaCO<sub>3</sub>]
questions.explanation: Pure solids (and pure liquids) have essentially constant molar concentration (density/molar mass) and are omitted from the equilibrium expression; their constant value is absorbed into K<sub>c</sub>. Only the gas, CO<sub>2</sub>, appears.
questions.hint: Only species whose concentration can actually change should appear in K.
distractor_logic: Wrongly includes only one of the two solids while still omitting the gas incorrectly
Inverts the expression and still includes solids
Wrongly includes the pure solids CaCO<sub>3</sub> and CaO as if they were variable-concentration species

questions.question: Which of the following is a heterogeneous equilibrium?
options: 2SO<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) ↔ 2SO<sub>3</sub>(g)
H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ↔ 2HI(g)
N<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) ↔ 2NO(g)
Ni(s) + 4CO(g) ↔ Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>(g)
questions.explanation: Ni(s) + 4CO(g) ↔ Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>(g) involves a solid (Ni) and gases together, so it is heterogeneous. The other three reactions have every species in the gas phase, making them homogeneous.
questions.hint: Look for a solid or liquid mixed in with gases.
distractor_logic: All-gas reaction — homogeneous
All-gas reaction — homogeneous
All-gas reaction — homogeneous

questions.question: The reaction quotient Q<sub>c</sub> is calculated using the same expression as K<sub>c</sub>, but:
options: Only when a catalyst is present
Using concentrations at any stage of the reaction, not necessarily at equilibrium
Only for gas-phase reactions
Only at equilibrium
questions.explanation: Q<sub>c</sub> has the identical mathematical form as K<sub>c</sub> but is evaluated using whatever concentrations exist at a given moment, letting us judge how far the system is from equilibrium by comparing Q<sub>c</sub> to K<sub>c</sub>.
questions.hint: Q is a snapshot; K is the equilibrium value.
distractor_logic: Catalysts are irrelevant to whether Q can be calculated
Q<sub>c</sub> can be written for any reaction with a defined equilibrium expression, gas-phase or not
This describes K<sub>c</sub>, not Q<sub>c</sub> — the whole point of Q is that it isn't restricted to equilibrium

questions.question: If Q<sub>c</sub> < K<sub>c</sub> for a reaction at a given instant, the reaction will proceed:
options: In the reverse direction, to form more reactants
In the forward direction, to form more products
Not at all, since it is already at equilibrium
In both directions simultaneously at equal rates
questions.explanation: Q<sub>c</sub> < K<sub>c</sub> means there are proportionally too few products (or too many reactants) compared to the equilibrium ratio, so the forward reaction proceeds net to increase products until Q rises to meet K.
questions.hint: If Q is smaller than K, which side needs to 'catch up'?
distractor_logic: This is the correct trend, but placed at the wrong index as a distractor check is not needed here
This is the opposite direction; Q<K pushes the reaction forward, not backward
Q<sub>c</sub> = K<sub>c</sub> only exactly at equilibrium, not when they differ

questions.question: The relationship between K<sub>p</sub> and K<sub>c</sub> for a gas-phase reaction is given by:
options: K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub>(RT)<sup>−1</sup>, always
K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub> / Δn
K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub> + Δn RT
K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub>(RT)<sup>Δn</sup>
questions.explanation: K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub>(RT)<sup>Δn</sup>, where Δn = (moles of gaseous products) − (moles of gaseous reactants), R is the gas constant, and T is the absolute temperature.
questions.hint: The exponent is Δn, not a fixed number.
distractor_logic: Fixes the exponent at −1 instead of letting it equal the actual Δn of the reaction
Divides instead of raising to a power
Turns a multiplicative power-law relation into an additive one — dimensionally and mathematically wrong

questions.question: In the relation K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub>(RT)<sup>Δn</sup>, the symbol Δn represents:
options: (moles of gaseous products) − (moles of gaseous reactants), from the balanced equation
The number of moles of catalyst used
The change in temperature during the reaction
The total number of moles of gas present at equilibrium
questions.explanation: Δn is purely a stoichiometric quantity taken from the balanced equation's gas-phase species: products' gas moles minus reactants' gas moles. It has nothing to do with actual amounts present or with temperature change.
questions.hint: It's a count from the equation, not from the reaction vessel.
distractor_logic: Catalysts don't appear in equilibrium expressions or in Δn at all
Δn is a mole count, not a temperature term — T appears separately in the formula
Confuses Δn (a fixed stoichiometric number) with the actual total moles present, which does depend on how much reacted

questions.question: For a gas-phase reaction with Δn = 0 (equal moles of gas on both sides, e.g. H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ↔ 2HI(g)):
options: K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub>
K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub> × RT
K<sub>p</sub> is always exactly zero
K<sub>p</sub> and K<sub>c</sub> cannot be compared
questions.explanation: Since (RT)<sup>Δn</sup> = (RT)<sup>0</sup> = 1 when Δn = 0, the relation K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub>(RT)<sup>Δn</sup> reduces to K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub> exactly, with no unit or temperature dependence entering the comparison.
questions.hint: What is (RT) raised to the power zero?
distractor_logic: Forgets that (RT)<sup>0</sup> = 1, not RT
Confuses zero exponent with a zero value of K itself
The whole point of the K<sub>p</sub>-K<sub>c</sub> relation is that they ARE comparable via Δn

questions.question: Le Chatelier's principle states that when a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in concentration, pressure, or temperature, the equilibrium shifts in a direction that:
options: Has no effect on the position of equilibrium
Partially counteracts the effect of that change
Always favours the formation of products
Increases the disturbance further
questions.explanation: Le Chatelier's principle: a system at equilibrium responds to an applied stress (change in concentration, pressure/volume, or temperature) by shifting in the direction that tends to reduce or partially offset that stress, reaching a new equilibrium position.
questions.hint: The system 'pushes back' against the change.
distractor_logic: Contradicts the entire premise of the principle — equilibrium position does shift
Overgeneralises; the shift can favour reactants or products depending on the specific stress applied
This is the opposite of Le Chatelier's principle

questions.question: Adding an inert gas (like argon) to a gaseous equilibrium at constant volume:
options: Shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas
Shifts the equilibrium towards the side with more moles of gas
Has no effect on the equilibrium position, since partial pressures of reacting species are unchanged
Always shifts the equilibrium completely to products
questions.explanation: At constant volume, adding an inert gas increases total pressure but does not change the partial pressures (or concentrations) of the reacting gases, since their moles per unit volume are unaffected. Q<sub>c</sub> still equals K<sub>c</sub>, so there is no shift.
questions.hint: Does the inert gas change how many molecules of the actual reactants/products are squeezed into the same volume?
distractor_logic: Same reasoning error as above, wrong direction
This would be true only if the inert gas addition were done at constant pressure (which increases volume)
Confuses inert-gas addition with a genuine change in the reacting species' concentrations

questions.question: For an exothermic reaction at equilibrium, increasing the temperature will:
options: Increase both the forward and reverse rate constants equally, leaving equilibrium position unchanged
Shift the equilibrium in the forward (product-forming) direction, increasing K
Shift the equilibrium in the reverse direction, decreasing K
Have no effect on the equilibrium position or K
questions.explanation: Heat behaves like a 'product' in an exothermic reaction. Raising temperature adds to that side, so by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic (reverse) direction to absorb the extra heat, and K decreases.
questions.hint: In an exothermic reaction, heat is released — so which side does raising T push the reaction toward?
distractor_logic: Rate constants for forward and reverse do not increase equally in general, and equilibrium position is not unaffected by T
This is the correct behaviour for an endothermic reaction, not an exothermic one — the two are commonly swapped
K does change with temperature; it is only independent of concentration/pressure changes, not of T

questions.question: Adding a catalyst to a reaction at equilibrium:
options: Has no effect on either the forward or the reverse reaction rate
Speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally and helps equilibrium to be attained faster, without shifting its position
Increases K<sub>c</sub> and shifts equilibrium toward products
Decreases K<sub>c</sub> and shifts equilibrium toward reactants
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy for both the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount, so both rates increase equally. Equilibrium is reached sooner, but the equilibrium concentrations (and K<sub>c</sub>) are completely unchanged.
questions.hint: A catalyst is about speed, not position — this is one of the most tested traps in this chapter.
distractor_logic: A catalyst definitely affects both rates (that's its entire function); it just affects them equally
A catalyst never changes the value of K<sub>c</sub>, regardless of framing
Same error in the opposite direction — catalysts do not shift equilibrium position at all

questions.topic: Acids, Bases and the Lewis Concept
questions.question: According to the Bronsted-Lowry concept, an acid is defined as a species that:
options: Donates a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) to another species
Accepts a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) from another species
Accepts a pair of electrons
Donates a pair of electrons
questions.explanation: Bronsted-Lowry: an acid is a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) donor, and a base is a proton acceptor. This is broader than the Arrhenius definition, which requires the acid to specifically release H<sup>+</sup> in aqueous solution.
questions.hint: Bronsted = proton transfer.
distractor_logic: This defines a Bronsted-Lowry base, not an acid — donor and acceptor are swapped
This is the Lewis definition of an acid, not the Bronsted-Lowry one
This is the Lewis definition of a base, not the Bronsted-Lowry definition of an acid

questions.topic: Acids, Bases and the Lewis Concept
questions.question: In the reaction NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ↔ NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>−</sup>, the conjugate acid-base pairs are:
options: There are no conjugate pairs in this reaction
NH<sub>3</sub>/NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> and H<sub>2</sub>O/OH<sup>−</sup>
NH<sub>3</sub>/OH<sup>−</sup> and H<sub>2</sub>O/NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>
NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>/OH<sup>−</sup> only
questions.explanation: A conjugate acid-base pair differs by exactly one proton. NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> is NH<sub>3</sub> plus a proton (its conjugate acid), and H<sub>2</sub>O is OH<sup>−</sup> plus a proton (H<sub>2</sub>O is the conjugate acid of OH<sup>−</sup>).
questions.hint: Pair each species with the one that differs from it by a single H<sup>+</sup>.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly claims no conjugate relationship exists in an acid-base proton-transfer reaction
Cross-pairs species that don't actually differ by one proton from each other
Only names one pair and ignores that NH<sub>3</sub>/NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> is also a conjugate pair

questions.topic: Acids, Bases and the Lewis Concept
questions.question: According to the Lewis concept, a base is a species that:
options: Donates an electron pair to form a coordinate bond
Donates a proton
Accepts a proton
Accepts an electron pair to form a coordinate bond
questions.explanation: The Lewis definition is the most general: a Lewis base is an electron-pair donor and a Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor, which extends acid-base behaviour beyond proton transfer (e.g. BF<sub>3</sub> as a Lewis acid, NH<sub>3</sub> as a Lewis base).
questions.hint: Lewis focuses on electron pairs, not protons.
distractor_logic: This is the Bronsted-Lowry definition of an acid, not the Lewis definition of a base
This is the Bronsted-Lowry definition of a base restated in proton language, not the Lewis (electron-pair) definition
This describes a Lewis acid, not a Lewis base — donor and acceptor are swapped

questions.topic: Ionization of Weak Acids and Bases
questions.question: For a weak acid HA that partially ionises as HA ↔ H<sup>+</sup> + A<sup>−</sup>, the acid ionization constant K<sub>a</sub> is written as:
options: K<sub>a</sub> = [HA] / [H<sup>+</sup>][A<sup>−</sup>]
K<sub>a</sub> = [H<sup>+</sup>] + [A<sup>−</sup>] − [HA]
K<sub>a</sub> = [HA][H<sup>+</sup>][A<sup>−</sup>]
K<sub>a</sub> = [H<sup>+</sup>][A<sup>−</sup>] / [HA]
questions.explanation: Like any equilibrium constant, K<sub>a</sub> is products over reactants at equilibrium: the ionised products H<sup>+</sup> and A<sup>−</sup> in the numerator, the undissociated acid HA in the denominator.
questions.hint: Same law-of-mass-action pattern as any other K.
distractor_logic: Inverts the correct expression
Adds/subtracts concentrations instead of forming the products-over-reactants ratio
Multiplies instead of dividing

questions.topic: Ionization of Weak Acids and Bases
questions.question: A larger value of K<sub>a</sub> for a weak acid indicates that the acid is:
options: A stronger acid, ionising to a greater extent
Exactly as strong as a typical strong acid like HCl
A weaker acid, ionising to a lesser extent
Not an acid at all
questions.explanation: K<sub>a</sub> measures the extent of ionisation at equilibrium. A larger K<sub>a</sub> means the equilibrium lies further toward H<sup>+</sup> and A<sup>−</sup>, i.e. the acid is stronger (more ionised) among weak acids.
questions.hint: Bigger K<sub>a</sub>, more ionisation — same logic as any equilibrium constant.
distractor_logic: Strong acids like HCl are considered to ionise essentially completely and are not assigned a finite K<sub>a</sub> in the same comparative sense
Reverses the correct trend
K<sub>a</sub> is only defined for species that do ionise as acids, so this option is inconsistent with the premise

questions.topic: Ionization of Weak Acids and Bases
questions.question: For a conjugate acid-base pair in water, the relationship between K<sub>a</sub> (of the acid) and K<sub>b</sub> (of its conjugate base) is:
options: K<sub>a</sub> + K<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>w</sub>
K<sub>a</sub> = K<sub>b</sub> always
K<sub>a</sub> × K<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>w</sub>
K<sub>a</sub> − K<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>w</sub>
questions.explanation: For any conjugate acid-base pair, K<sub>a</sub> × K<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>w</sub> (the ionic product of water, 10<sup>−14</sup> at 25°C). This links how strong an acid is to how weak its conjugate base must be, and vice versa.
questions.hint: Multiply, don't add, the two constants.
distractor_logic: Uses addition instead of multiplication
K<sub>a</sub> and K<sub>b</sub> of a conjugate pair are generally very different (a strong-ish acid has a very weak conjugate base)
Uses subtraction instead of multiplication

questions.topic: Ionic Product of Water and the pH Scale
questions.question: The ionic product of water, K<sub>w</sub> = [H<sup>+</sup>][OH<sup>−</sup>], has the value at 25°C of:
options: 10<sup>−7</sup>
10<sup>−14</sup>
10<sup>−1</sup>
questions.explanation: At 25°C, pure water has [H<sup>+</sup>] = [OH<sup>−</sup>] = 10<sup>−7</sup> M, so K<sub>w</sub> = (10<sup>−7</sup>)(10<sup>−7</sup>) = 10<sup>−14</sup>.
questions.hint: K<sub>w</sub> is the product of two 10<sup>−7</sup> terms, not one of them alone.
distractor_logic: Mistakes [H<sup>+</sup>] itself (or [OH<sup>−</sup>] itself) in pure water for the full product K<sub>w</sub>
Garbles the power-of-ten arithmetic when multiplying two 10<sup>−7</sup> terms together (10<sup>−7</sup> × 10<sup>−7</sup> = 10<sup>−14</sup>, not 10<sup>−1</sup>)
Confuses K<sub>w</sub> with an unrelated round number

questions.topic: Ionic Product of Water and the pH Scale
questions.question: pH is defined as:
options: pH = log[H<sup>+</sup>]
pH = log[OH<sup>−</sup>]
pH = −log[H<sup>+</sup>]
pH = 1/[H<sup>+</sup>]
questions.explanation: pH is defined as the negative logarithm (base 10) of the hydrogen ion concentration: pH = −log[H<sup>+</sup>]. The minus sign is essential since [H<sup>+</sup>] is normally less than 1, making log[H<sup>+</sup>] negative; pH itself should read as a small positive number for acids.
questions.hint: Without the minus sign, acidic solutions would show a negative pH.
distractor_logic: Drops the essential minus sign, which flips the whole scale
Uses [OH<sup>−</sup>] where [H<sup>+</sup>] is required — that would define pOH-like quantity incorrectly
Confuses the logarithmic definition with a simple reciprocal

questions.topic: Ionic Product of Water and the pH Scale
questions.question: At 25°C, a solution with pH less than 7 is:
options: Impossible, since pH cannot be less than 7
Acidic
Basic (alkaline)
Neutral
questions.explanation: At 25°C, neutral water has pH = 7. A pH below 7 means [H<sup>+</sup>] > 10<sup>−7</sup> M, which defines an acidic solution; pH above 7 is basic.
questions.hint: Lower pH corresponds to a higher [H<sup>+</sup>].
distractor_logic: pH can range from below 0 to above 14 for very concentrated solutions; it is not bounded below by 7
Reverses acidic and basic on the pH scale
Confuses acidic (pH<7) with neutral (pH=7)

questions.topic: Degree of Dissociation and Ostwald's Dilution Law
questions.question: The degree of dissociation (α) of a weak electrolyte is defined as:
options: The equilibrium constant of the dissociation reaction
The total concentration of the electrolyte taken initially
The number of ions produced per formula unit
The fraction of the total amount of electrolyte that has dissociated into ions at equilibrium
questions.explanation: α is a fraction (0 to 1) representing what proportion of the originally dissolved weak electrolyte has ionised at equilibrium; (1−α) remains undissociated.
questions.hint: α is a fraction, not a concentration or a constant.
distractor_logic: Confuses α (a fraction of dissociation) with K<sub>a</sub> or K<sub>b</sub> (an equilibrium constant)
Confuses α with the total initial concentration, C, which is a separate quantity
Confuses α with the stoichiometric number of ions (e.g. 2 for a 1:1 salt), a fixed integer property of the formula

questions.topic: Degree of Dissociation and Ostwald's Dilution Law
questions.question: Ostwald's dilution law predicts that for a weak electrolyte, the degree of dissociation (α):
options: Decreases on dilution
Becomes zero on dilution
Increases on dilution (approaches 1 at infinite dilution)
Stays exactly constant regardless of dilution
questions.explanation: Ostwald's dilution law gives α ≈ √(K<sub>a</sub>/C) for small α, so as concentration C decreases (more dilute), α increases — weak electrolytes dissociate more as they are diluted, approaching complete dissociation at infinite dilution.
questions.hint: α and concentration C move in opposite directions.
distractor_logic: Reverses the correct dilution trend
The extreme opposite error — dilution increases, not eliminates, dissociation
Contradicts the entire premise of Ostwald's dilution law, which is precisely about how α changes with dilution

questions.question: The common ion effect refers to the phenomenon in which:
options: Adding an ion already present in an equilibrium mixture suppresses the ionisation/dissolution of a weak electrolyte or sparingly soluble salt
The common ion effect only applies to strong electrolytes
Any ion addition always shifts equilibrium toward more dissociation
Adding an ion already present increases the ionisation of a weak electrolyte
questions.explanation: By Le Chatelier's principle, adding an ion that is already a product of an equilibrium (a 'common ion') shifts that equilibrium backward, suppressing further ionisation or dissolution — e.g. adding acetate ion suppresses acetic acid's ionisation.
questions.hint: Le Chatelier's principle applied specifically to a shared ion.
distractor_logic: The common ion effect is most dramatically seen with weak electrolytes and sparingly soluble salts, not strong electrolytes which are already fully dissociated
Overgeneralises; only a common ion (already part of that specific equilibrium) causes this suppression
Reverses the direction of the shift — the common ion suppresses, it does not promote, further ionisation

questions.question: Adding sodium acetate (CH<sub>3</sub>COONa) to a solution of acetic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) will:
options: Have no effect on the ionisation of acetic acid
Convert all the acetic acid into acetate ion
Increase the degree of dissociation of acetic acid
Decrease the degree of dissociation of acetic acid, due to the common acetate ion

options: Has a pH of exactly 7 under all conditions
Resists significant change in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added
Cannot be prepared in the laboratory
Is always made from a strong acid and a strong base

questions.question: For the exothermic reaction N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 3H<sub>2</sub>(g) ↔ 2NH<sub>3</sub>(g) (ΔH < 0), which change will increase the equilibrium yield of NH<sub>3</sub>?

questions.question: 1.0 mol H<sub>2</sub> and 1.0 mol I<sub>2</sub> are placed in a 1 L flask at a temperature where K<sub>c</sub> = 64 for H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ↔ 2HI(g). If x mol of H<sub>2</sub> reacts, what are the equilibrium concentrations of H<sub>2</sub>, I<sub>2</sub>, and HI?
questions.explanation: ICE: [H<sub>2</sub>]=[I<sub>2</sub>]=1−x, [HI]=2x. K<sub>c</sub>=(2x)<sup>2</sup>/(1−x)<sup>2</sup>=64 ⇒ 2x/(1−x)=8 (taking the positive square root) ⇒ 2x=8−8x ⇒ 10x=8 ⇒ x=0.8. So [H<sub>2</sub>]=[I<sub>2</sub>]=1−0.8=0.2 M and [HI]=2(0.8)=1.6 M. Check: (1.6)<sup>2</sup>/(0.2×0.2)=2.56/0.04=64 ✓

questions.topic: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constant
questions.question: 1.0 mol PCl<sub>5</sub> is introduced into a 1 L flask and allowed to reach equilibrium: PCl<sub>5</sub>(g) ↔ PCl<sub>3</sub>(g) + Cl<sub>2</sub>(g), with K<sub>c</sub> = 0.36. What fraction of the PCl<sub>5</sub> dissociates (α) at equilibrium?
questions.explanation: ICE with C<sub>0</sub>=1: [PCl<sub>5</sub>]=1−α, [PCl<sub>3</sub>]=[Cl<sub>2</sub>]=α. K<sub>c</sub>=α<sup>2</sup>/(1−α)=0.36 ⇒ α<sup>2</sup>+0.36α−0.36=0. Solving the quadratic: α = [−0.36+√(0.36<sup>2</sup>+4(0.36))]/2 ≈ 0.446, i.e. ≈ 45%. This large α means the simple 'Cα<sup>2</sup> ≈ K' shortcut (valid only for small α) cannot be used here — the full quadratic is required.
questions.hint: Here α is not small (C<sub>0</sub>=1 makes it comparable to Kc), so solve the full quadratic rather than approximating (1−α)≈1.
distractor_logic: Simply reports K<sub>c</sub> itself as if it were α, coincidentally close in this specific case but not derived correctly
Overcorrects by roughly doubling the true root of the quadratic
Uses the invalid small-α shortcut α≈√K<sub>c</sub>/C<sub>0</sub> here, which underestimates α because it wrongly approximates (1−α) as 1

questions.question: At a certain high temperature, K<sub>p</sub> for CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) ↔ CaO(s) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g) is 0.05 atm (i.e. the equilibrium CO<sub>2</sub> pressure is 0.05 atm) in a rigid, evacuated 10 L vessel at 1073 K. Using R = 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> and molar mass of CaCO<sub>3</sub> = 100 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, approximately what mass of CaCO<sub>3</sub> must decompose to establish this equilibrium?
options: ≈ 0.57 g
≈ 0.057 g
≈ 57 g
≈ 5.7 g

Using PV = nRT: n(CO<sub>2</sub>) = PV/RT = (0.05 × 10)/(0.0821 × 1073) ≈ 0.00568 mol. Since 1 mol CaCO<sub>3</sub> gives 1 mol CO<sub>2</sub>, mass of CaCO<sub>3</sub> decomposed = 0.00568 × 100 ≈ 0.57 g.
questions.hint: K<sub>p</sub> here IS simply the equilibrium partial pressure of the one gas involved — use PV=nRT to get moles of CO<sub>2</sub>, then convert to grams of CaCO<sub>3</sub> via 1:1 stoichiometry.

questions.question: For N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 3H<sub>2</sub>(g) ↔ 2NH<sub>3</sub>(g), K<sub>p</sub> = 1.5 × 10<sup>−5</sup> at a given temperature. At some instant, the partial pressures are P(N<sub>2</sub>) = 1 atm, P(H<sub>2</sub>) = 3 atm, and P(NH<sub>3</sub>) = 0.5 atm. In which direction will the reaction proceed?
options: Forward, since Q<sub>p</sub> ≈ 9.3 × 10<sup>−3</sup>, which is much less than K<sub>p</sub>
The system is already at equilibrium

Reverse, since Q<sub>p</sub> ≈ 9.3 × 10<sup>−3</sup>, which is much greater than K<sub>p</sub>

Since Q<sub>p</sub> (≈9.3 × 10<sup>−3</sup>) is far larger than K<sub>p</sub> (1.5 × 10<sup>−5</sup>), too much NH<sub>3</sub> is present relative to equilibrium, and the reaction must proceed in reverse to consume some of it.
questions.hint: Cube P(H<sub>2</sub>) in the denominator — a very common place to under-count the exponent.

questions.question: For H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ↔ 2HI(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 54 at 425°C. At some instant during the reaction, [H<sub>2</sub>] = 0.10 M, [I<sub>2</sub>] = 0.20 M, and [HI] = 1.00 M. Which of the following correctly describes the system and predicts what happens next?

Q<sub>c</sub> cannot be found without knowing the total volume of the container
Q<sub>c</sub> = 50, which is greater than K<sub>c</sub> = 54, so the reverse reaction dominates

questions.hint: Compute Q<sub>c</sub> precisely first, then judge both the direction AND how close the system already is to equilibrium.
distractor_logic: Makes an arithmetic slip in computing Q<sub>c</sub> (dividing incorrectly) and overstates how far from equilibrium the system is

questions.question: For PCl<sub>5</sub>(g) ↔ PCl<sub>3</sub>(g) + Cl<sub>2</sub>(g), K<sub>p</sub> = 1.8 at 500 K. First convert this to K<sub>c</sub> (R = 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>), then use that K<sub>c</sub> to find the degree of dissociation α if 0.5 mol of PCl<sub>5</sub> is placed in a 1 L flask.
options: K<sub>c</sub> ≈ 0.0438; α ≈ 0.256 (25.6%)
K<sub>c</sub> ≈ 73.9; α ≈ 0.90 (90%)
K<sub>c</sub> ≈ 1.8; α ≈ 0.44 (44%)
K<sub>c</sub> ≈ 0.0438; α ≈ 0.66 (66%)
questions.explanation: Step 1: Δn = +1, so K<sub>c</sub> = K<sub>p</sub>/(RT) = 1.8/(0.0821 × 500) = 1.8/41.05 ≈ 0.0438. Step 2: with C<sub>0</sub> = 0.5 M, K<sub>c</sub> = C<sub>0</sub>α<sup>2</sup>/(1−α) ⇒ 0.5α<sup>2</sup>+0.0438α−0.0438=0. Solving the quadratic gives α ≈ 0.256, i.e. about 25.6%.
questions.hint: This is a two-stage problem: first strip out (RT) to get K<sub>c</sub>, then plug that K<sub>c</sub> into the usual ICE/α quadratic — don't skip straight from K<sub>p</sub> to α.

questions.question: At a certain temperature, K for A(g) ↔ B(g) is 4, and K for B(g) ↔ C(g) is 9. What is K for the overall reaction A(g) ↔ C(g) at that same temperature?
questions.explanation: When two equilibria are added together (A↔B, then B↔C, giving A↔C overall), the overall equilibrium constant is the PRODUCT of the individual K values (this follows from multiplying the two K-expressions, which cancels [B]): K(A↔C) = K<sub>1</sub> × K<sub>2</sub> = 4 × 9 = 36.
questions.hint: When equilibria are combined by addition, their K values multiply — they do not add.
distractor_logic: Divides one K by the other instead of multiplying them
Takes the reciprocal of the product, as if computing K for the reverse of the combined reaction
Adds the two K values instead of multiplying them

questions.question: For 2NH<sub>3</sub>(g) ↔ N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 3H<sub>2</sub>(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 2.0 at 300 K. What is K<sub>p</sub> for this reaction (R = 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>)?
options: ≈ 49.3
≈ 2.0
≈ 1213
questions.explanation: Δn = (1+3) − 2 = +2 for this (reverse-of-ammonia-synthesis) reaction. K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub>(RT)<sup>Δn</sup> = 2.0 × (0.0821 × 300)<sup>2</sup> = 2.0 × (24.63)<sup>2</sup> ≈ 2.0 × 606.6 ≈ 1213.
questions.hint: Δn = +2 here (not −2, since this is written as ammonia decomposing, the reverse of the usual synthesis direction) — square (RT), don't take its square root.

questions.question: For the exothermic reaction N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 3H<sub>2</sub>(g) ↔ 2NH<sub>3</sub>(g), which combination of conditions would give the HIGHEST equilibrium yield of NH<sub>3</sub>?
options: Low temperature and low pressure
Low temperature and high pressure
High temperature and low pressure
High temperature and high pressure
questions.explanation: Two separate stresses act in the same helpful direction here: lowering temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction (Le Chatelier, heat-as-product logic), and raising pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles, which is also the product (NH<sub>3</sub>) side (4 mol gas → 2 mol gas). Combining low T and high P therefore reinforces each other for maximum yield (in industrial practice, a moderate compromise temperature is used for reaction rate, but the equilibrium-yield argument alone favours low T).
questions.hint: Work out the favourable direction for temperature and for pressure SEPARATELY first, then find the option where both point the same way.
distractor_logic: Low P favours the reactant (more-mole) side, working against yield even though low T still helps
Both conditions here work against maximum NH<sub>3</sub> yield
High T favours the reverse (endothermic) direction, working against yield even though high P still helps

questions.question: For N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(g) ↔ 2NO<sub>2</sub>(g), K<sub>p</sub> = 0.144 atm. Using K<sub>p</sub> = 4α<sup>2</sup>P/(1−α<sup>2</sup>) (starting from pure N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>), the degree of dissociation α at total pressure P = 1 atm is ≈ 0.186. If the total pressure is instead raised to P = 4 atm at the same temperature, α becomes approximately:
options: 0.744 (dissociation increases sharply with pressure)
0.094 (dissociation is suppressed by the higher pressure)
0.186 (unchanged, since K<sub>p</sub> is fixed)
0.372 (dissociation doubles with pressure)
questions.explanation: Rearranging, α = √(K<sub>p</sub>/(4P+K<sub>p</sub>)). At P=4: α = √(0.144/(16+0.144)) ≈ √(0.00893) ≈ 0.094. Increasing pressure suppresses dissociation (fewer moles of gas favoured), consistent with N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> → 2NO<sub>2</sub> being the mole-increasing direction, which Le Chatelier's principle says high pressure opposes — confirmed quantitatively here since α roughly halves.
questions.hint: Even though K<sub>p</sub> stays fixed with pressure, α itself is NOT fixed — it must be recomputed from the K<sub>p</sub>-P-α relation at the new pressure.
distractor_logic: Gets the direction of the pressure effect backwards; higher pressure should suppress, not enhance, dissociation into more moles of gas
Confuses K<sub>p</sub> being constant with temperature with α being constant with pressure — they are not the same thing
Assumes α simply scales in direct proportion to P, which isn't how the P appears inside the square root

questions.question: H<sub>2</sub>S is a diprotic acid with K<sub>a1</sub> = 1.0 × 10<sup>−7</sup> and K<sub>a2</sub> = 1.3 × 10<sup>−13</sup>. In a 0.1 M H<sub>2</sub>S solution, what are [H<sup>+</sup>] and [S<sup>2−</sup>] approximately?
options: [H<sup>+</sup>] ≈ 1.0 × 10<sup>−7</sup> M; [S<sup>2−</sup>] ≈ 1.0 × 10<sup>−7</sup> M
[H<sup>+</sup>] ≈ 1.3 × 10<sup>−13</sup> M; [S<sup>2−</sup>] ≈ 1.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> M

In the second step, HS<sup>−</sup> ↔ H<sup>+</sup> + S<sup>2−</sup>, K<sub>a2</sub> = [H<sup>+</sup>][S<sup>2−</sup>]/[HS<sup>−</sup>]. questions.topic: Ionic Product of Water and the pH Scale
questions.question: Equal volumes of a solution with pH = 2 and a solution with pH = 4 (both strong acids) are mixed. What is the pH of the resulting mixture?

≈ 2.70
≈ 1.70

questions.question: 10 mL of 1 M HCl is diluted with water to a final volume of 1 L. What is the pH of the diluted solution?

questions.question: 50 mL of 0.1 M HCl is mixed with 50 mL of 0.08 M NaOH. What is the pH of the resulting solution?

The acid is in slight excess, so the solution remains acidic, not neutral.

questions.question: A weak acid has K<sub>a</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup> and is present at C = 0.001 M (quite dilute). Comparing the simple approximation α ≈ √(K<sub>a</sub>/C) with the exact quadratic solution of Cα<sup>2</sup>/(1−α) = K<sub>a</sub>, which statement is correct?

Approximate α ≈ 0.134, exact α ≈ 0.125 — a difference of about 7%, so the simple approximation is no longer very reliable at this low concentration

questions.question: For the same relationship α<sub>1</sub>/α<sub>2</sub> = √(C<sub>2</sub>/C<sub>1</sub>), a different weak acid has α<sub>1</sub> = 0.02 at C<sub>1</sub> = 0.2 M. After diluting to C<sub>2</sub> = 0.002 M (again a 100-fold dilution), α<sub>2</sub> becomes:

questions.question: 0.1 M CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (K<sub>a</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>) is mixed with enough HCl to make the solution 0.05 M in HCl as well. Since HCl is a strong acid, [H<sup>+</sup>] ≈ 0.05 M (essentially fixed by the HCl). Using α ≈ K<sub>a</sub>/[H<sup>+</sup>], by what rough factor is the acetic acid's own degree of ionisation suppressed compared to 0.1 M acetic acid alone (α ≈ 0.0134 alone)?

Suppressed to ≈ 3.6 × 10<sup>−4</sup>, roughly a 37-fold reduction
Suppressed to ≈ 1.34 × 10<sup>−3</sup>, essentially unchanged
Increased to ≈ 0.05, since more H<sup>+</sup> promotes more ionisation
questions.explanation: α ≈ K<sub>a</sub>/[H<sup>+</sup>] = (1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>)/0.05 = 3.6 × 10<sup>−4</sup>, compared to α ≈ 0.0134 for 0.1 M acetic acid alone — a reduction of roughly 0.0134/0.00036 ≈ 37-fold, since the strong acid's H<sup>+</sup> (a common ion in the acetic acid equilibrium) massively suppresses the weak acid's own ionisation.
questions.hint: Once a strong acid fixes [H<sup>+</sup>] at a much higher level than the weak acid alone would produce, α of the weak acid can be estimated directly as K<sub>a</sub>/[H<sup>+</sup>] (from its own equilibrium expression, since [H<sup>+</sup>] is now externally controlled).

Reports a value close to the unsuppressed α, missing that a strong acid's H<sup>+</sup> is a common ion that suppresses the weak acid's own ionisation much more strongly than shown
Reverses the entire logic of the common ion effect — MORE common H<sup>+</sup> suppresses, it does not promote, further ionisation of the weak acid

questions.question: The K<sub>sp</sub> of AgCl is 1.8 × 10<sup>−10</sup>. What is the molar solubility of AgCl in a 0.1 M NaCl solution (assume [Cl<sup>−</sup>] ≈ 0.1 M, dominated by the NaCl), and by roughly what factor is this lower than its solubility in pure water (≈ 1.34 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M)?

s ≈ 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M, slightly higher than in pure water

s ≈ 1.34 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M, unchanged from pure water

questions.question: For 0.1 M CH<sub>3</sub>COONa (K<sub>a</sub> of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>, K<sub>w</sub> = 1.0 × 10<sup>−14</sup>), find the hydrolysis constant K<sub>h</sub> and the approximate degree of hydrolysis h, using K<sub>h</sub> = K<sub>w</sub>/K<sub>a</sub> and h ≈ √(K<sub>h</sub>/C).

questions.question: A salt is formed from a weak acid with pK<sub>a</sub> = 5 and a weak base with pK<sub>b</sub> = 3. Using pH = 7 + ½pK<sub>a</sub> − ½pK<sub>b</sub>, what is the pH of its aqueous solution, and is it acidic or basic?

pH = 7.0; neutral, since it's a salt of a weak acid and weak base
pH = 8.0; basic, because the base (pK<sub>b</sub>=3) is stronger than the acid (pK<sub>a</sub>=5) is weak
pH = 6.0; slightly acidic
questions.explanation: pH = 7 + ½(5) − ½(3) = 7 + 2.5 − 1.5 = 8.0. A smaller pK<sub>b</sub> means the conjugate base's parent (the weak base) is comparatively stronger (more willing to accept protons back), pulling the solution basic rather than neutral.
questions.hint: This formula is only pH = 7 (neutral) when pK<sub>a</sub> = pK<sub>b</sub> exactly — here they differ, so the pH shifts away from 7 in the direction of the STRONGER parent (smaller pK value).

Gets the right general idea that it's near neutral but miscalculates the half-differences

questions.question: A buffer contains 0.1 M CH<sub>3</sub>COOH and 0.1 M CH<sub>3</sub>COONa in 1 L (pK<sub>a</sub> = 4.74). 0.01 mol of solid NaOH is added (assume negligible volume change). What is the new pH?
options: ≈ 4.83
≈ 4.74 (unchanged)
≈ 8.87
≈ 5.74
questions.explanation: NaOH consumes an equal amount of the acid form: new [CH<sub>3</sub>COOH] = 0.1−0.01 = 0.09 M, new [CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>] = 0.1+0.01 = 0.11 M. pH = 4.74 + log(0.11/0.09) = 4.74 + log(1.222) ≈ 4.74 + 0.087 ≈ 4.83. This small shift (from 4.74 to 4.83) demonstrates the buffer resisting a large pH change despite the added strong base.
questions.hint: Update BOTH the acid and salt concentrations (one decreases, the other increases by the same moles) before reapplying Henderson-Hasselbalch — don't just recompute from the original 1:1 ratio.
distractor_logic: Forgets that the buffer composition actually changed, simply reporting the original unbuffered pK<sub>a</sub> value
Computes the hydrolysis pH of pure sodium acetate instead of accounting for the fact that unreacted acetic acid still remains in this buffer
Treats the added NaOH as if it fully converted all the acid to salt (as in a full-neutralisation buffer-design problem), overshooting the small perturbation actually caused by only 0.01 mol

questions.question: You want to prepare an acetic acid/acetate buffer (pK<sub>a</sub> = 4.74) with pH = 5.74. What ratio of [CH<sub>3</sub>COONa] to [CH<sub>3</sub>COOH] is required?

questions.hint: Isolate log(ratio) first (it equals pH − pK<sub>a</sub>), then exponentiate both sides.
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio, giving acid in excess of salt when the higher target pH (above pK<sub>a</sub>) actually requires MORE salt (conjugate base) relative to acid
Underestimates the required ratio; a full order-of-magnitude difference in the ratio is needed for a full unit of pH change, not just a factor of 2
Assumes the target pH equals pK<sub>a</sub> (ratio 1:1), ignoring that 5.74 is one full pH unit above 4.74

questions.question: A basic buffer is made from NH<sub>4</sub>OH and NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (pK<sub>b</sub> of NH<sub>4</sub>OH = 4.74) with [NH<sub>4</sub>Cl]/[NH<sub>4</sub>OH] = 2. Using pOH = pK<sub>b</sub> + log([salt]/[base]), what is the pH of this buffer?

≈ 9.26
≈ 8.96
≈ 4.44

distractor_logic: Reports pOH (5.04) directly as if it were the pH, forgetting the final pH = 14 − pOH step
Same reasoning as NH<sub>4</sub>Cl salt hydrolysis pH — but this is a buffer question, not a bare salt hydrolysis question, so this value doesn't apply here
Reports pOH correctly as a number but subtracts it from the wrong reference or mislabels which quantity is which

questions.question: 50 mL of 0.001 M AgNO<sub>3</sub> is mixed with 50 mL of 0.001 M NaCl (K<sub>sp</sub> of AgCl = 1.8 × 10<sup>−10</sup>). After mixing, will a precipitate of AgCl form?

Cannot be determined without knowing the temperature

Q<sub>sp</sub> = (5 × 10<sup>−4</sup>)<sup>2</sup> = 2.5 × 10<sup>−7</sup>, which is far greater than K<sub>sp</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−10</sup>, so AgCl does precipitate until Q<sub>sp</sub> falls back to K<sub>sp</sub>.

questions.question: The K<sub>sp</sub> of CaF<sub>2</sub> is 3.9 × 10<sup>−11</sup>. What is the molar solubility of CaF<sub>2</sub> in a 0.01 M NaF solution (assume [F<sup>−</sup>] ≈ 0.01 M, dominated by NaF, so K<sub>sp</sub> ≈ s[F<sup>−</sup>]<sup>2</sup>)?
options: ≈ 1.0 × 10<sup>−2</sup> M
≈ 3.9 × 10<sup>−9</sup> M
≈ 3.9 × 10<sup>−7</sup> M
≈ 2.1 × 10<sup>−4</sup> M

questions.question: K<sub>sp</sub> of Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> is 5.6 × 10<sup>−12</sup>. Above what minimum pH will Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> just begin to precipitate from a solution containing 0.001 M Mg<sup>2+</sup>?

≈ 8.87
≈ 9.87
≈ 7.00

[OH<sup>−</sup>] = √(5.6 × 10<sup>−9</sup>) ≈ 7.48 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M, so pOH ≈ 4.13 and pH = 14 − 4.13 ≈ 9.87. Below this pH, Q<sub>sp</sub> stays under K<sub>sp</sub> and the solution remains clear.

questions.question: 100 mL of 0.002 M Pb(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> is mixed with 100 mL of 0.002 M KI (K<sub>sp</sub> of PbI<sub>2</sub>, an AB<sub>2</sub>-type salt, = 7.1 × 10<sup>−9</sup>). Will a precipitate of PbI<sub>2</sub> form?
options: Yes — the ion product clearly exceeds K<sub>sp</sub> once mixed
Cannot be determined since PbI<sub>2</sub> is an AB<sub>2</sub>-type salt, and Q<sub>sp</sub> rules don't apply to such salts

questions.question: For N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 3H<sub>2</sub>(g) ↔ 2NH<sub>3</sub>(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 0.5 at 400 K. Using K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub>(RT)<sup>Δn</sup>, K<sub>p</sub> ≈ 4.64 × 10<sup>−4</sup>. Since this reaction is exothermic, if the temperature were instead raised well above 400 K, what would happen to this K<sub>p</sub> value?
options: K<sub>p</sub> would stay at 4.64 × 10<sup>−4</sup>, since K<sub>p</sub> is temperature-independent
K<sub>p</sub> would become exactly equal to K<sub>c</sub>
K<sub>p</sub> would increase, since (RT)<sup>Δn</sup> always grows with T
K<sub>p</sub> would decrease, since raising temperature shifts an exothermic equilibrium in reverse, lowering both K<sub>c</sub> and K<sub>p</sub>
questions.explanation: Even though (RT)<sup>Δn</sup> is a mathematical factor in the K<sub>p</sub>-K<sub>c</sub> relation, K<sub>c</sub> ITSELF changes with temperature according to Le Chatelier's principle: for this exothermic reaction, raising T shifts equilibrium in reverse, which lowers K<sub>c</sub> substantially — and this drop in K<sub>c</sub> dominates over any change in the (RT)<sup>Δn</sup> factor (which here has a negative exponent, so it actually shrinks as T rises too), so K<sub>p</sub> decreases overall.
questions.hint: Don't just look at the (RT)<sup>Δn</sup> factor in isolation — remember K<sub>c</sub> itself is not fixed; it responds to temperature exactly as Le Chatelier's principle predicts for this exothermic reaction.
distractor_logic: Confuses temperature-independence of K<sub>c</sub> (a common but false assumption) — K only stays fixed when T is held constant, not across a temperature change
K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub> only when Δn = 0, which is not the case for this reaction (Δn = −2)
Wrongly assumes (RT)<sup>Δn</sup> alone dictates the trend without accounting for how K<sub>c</sub> itself shifts with temperature for an exothermic reaction

questions.question: For H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ↔ 2HI(g), Δn = 0, so K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub> at every temperature. If the total pressure on this equilibrium mixture is increased by decreasing the container volume at constant temperature, what happens to the equilibrium position and to K<sub>c</sub>?

The equilibrium shifts toward H<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>2</sub>, and K<sub>c</sub> decreases
K<sub>c</sub> becomes equal to K<sub>p</sub> for the first time under the new pressure
Neither shifts: equal gas moles on both sides means pressure changes don't favour either side, and K<sub>c</sub> is unaffected since temperature hasn't changed

And since K<sub>c</sub> depends only on temperature (which hasn't changed), K<sub>c</sub> itself is completely unaffected by the pressure change.
questions.hint: This is the Δn = 0 case from the K<sub>p</sub>-K<sub>c</sub> relation combined with the Le Chatelier rule that only unequal mole-counts respond to pressure changes — the two ideas reinforce each other here.
distractor_logic: Assumes pressure changes always favour product formation, ignoring that this specific reaction has equal gas moles on both sides

questions.question: For PCl<sub>5</sub>(g) ↔ PCl<sub>3</sub>(g) + Cl<sub>2</sub>(g), using K<sub>p</sub> = Pα<sup>2</sup>/(1−α<sup>2</sup>), α = 0.5 at total pressure P = 2 atm, giving K<sub>p</sub> ≈ 0.667. If the total pressure is instead raised to P = 8 atm at the same temperature (same K<sub>p</sub>), what happens to α, and is this consistent with Le Chatelier's principle?

α stays at 0.5, since K<sub>p</sub> is unchanged

questions.question: A buffer is made from NH<sub>4</sub>OH and NH<sub>4</sub>Cl, with K<sub>b</sub>(NH<sub>4</sub>OH) = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup> (not given directly as pK<sub>b</sub>) and [NH<sub>4</sub>Cl]/[NH<sub>4</sub>OH] = 4. What is the pH of this buffer?

No — at pH 9, [OH<sup>−</sup>] = 10<sup>−5</sup> M, giving Q<sub>sp</sub> = 1 × 10<sup>−12</sup>, which is less than K<sub>sp</sub>
