Q<sub>sp</sub> = [Mg<sup>2+</sup>][OH<sup>−</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = 0.01 × (10<sup>−5</sup>)<sup>2</sup> = 1 × 10<sup>−12</sup>, which is LESS than K<sub>sp</sub> = 5.6 × 10<sup>−12</sup>, so no precipitate forms at this pH (precipitation would require pH > ≈9.87, as found from setting Q<sub>sp</sub>=K<sub>sp</sub>).
questions.hint: Convert pH to [OH<sup>−</sup>] first, then compute Q<sub>sp</sub> and compare directly to K<sub>sp</sub> — don't rely on 'basic implies precipitation' as a shortcut.
distractor_logic: Wrongly treats 'basic pH' as automatically sufficient for precipitation without checking whether Q<sub>sp</sub> actually exceeds K<sub>sp</sub> for this specific concentration and K<sub>sp</sub>
The volume cancels out of the concentration-based Q<sub>sp</sub> comparison here; it is not needed since concentrations, not total moles, are what matter for K<sub>sp</sub>
Gets the right general setup but slips in comparing Q<sub>sp</sub> to K<sub>sp</sub>, concluding the opposite of what the actual numbers show
mixed_topics: Ionic Product of Water and the pH Scale

questions.topic: Degree of Dissociation and Ostwald's Dilution Law
questions.question: For an endothermic dissociation like PCl<sub>5</sub>(g) ↔ PCl<sub>3</sub>(g) + Cl<sub>2</sub>(g), raising temperature increases K<sub>c</sub> (Le Chatelier: heat favours the endothermic forward direction). If K<sub>c</sub> quadruples from 0.04 to 0.16 at constant C<sub>0</sub> = 0.5 M, how does α change?
options: α rises from ≈ 0.246 to ≈ 0.428 — less than doubling, even though K<sub>c</sub> quadrupled, because α depends on K<sub>c</sub> through a square-root-like (sub-linear) relationship
α decreases, since higher K<sub>c</sub> is associated with less dissociation
α stays the same, since C<sub>0</sub> hasn't changed
α also exactly quadruples, from ≈ 0.246 to ≈ 0.984
questions.explanation: Solving C<sub>0</sub>α<sup>2</sup>+K<sub>c</sub>α−K<sub>c</sub>=0 at each K<sub>c</sub>: for K<sub>c</sub>=0.04, α≈0.246; for K<sub>c</sub>=0.16, α≈0.428. So α does increase (correctly, per Le Chatelier, since higher K<sub>c</sub> means more dissociation), but by less than the factor of 4 that K<sub>c</sub> increased by, since the relationship between α and K<sub>c</sub> is not directly proportional.
questions.hint: Solve the quadratic separately for each K<sub>c</sub> value rather than assuming α scales in direct proportion to K<sub>c</sub>.
distractor_logic: Reverses the correct relationship — a larger K<sub>c</sub> means MORE dissociation (more products relative to reactant), not less
Ignores that K<sub>c</sub> did change here, when the whole scenario is built around K<sub>c</sub> increasing due to temperature
Correctly identifies that α increases with K<sub>c</sub> but wrongly assumes it scales by exactly the same factor as K<sub>c</sub> itself
mixed_topics: Degree of Dissociation and Ostwald's Dilution Law

questions.topic: Ionization of Weak Acids and Bases
questions.question: A 0.1 M NH<sub>3</sub> solution has K<sub>b</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>. What is its pH?
options: ≈ 11.13
≈ 4.74
≈ 9.26
≈ 2.87
questions.explanation: α ≈ √(K<sub>b</sub>/C) = √(1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>/0.1) ≈ 0.0134. [OH<sup>−</sup>] = Cα ≈ 0.1 × 0.0134 = 1.34 × 10<sup>−3</sup> M, so pOH ≈ 2.87, and pH = 14 − 2.87 ≈ 11.13.
questions.hint: This combines the Ostwald-style α calculation for a weak BASE with the pOH-to-pH conversion — don't stop at pOH.
distractor_logic: Reports the pK<sub>a</sub>/pK<sub>b</sub>-style value for acetic acid/ammonia rather than actually completing this specific pH calculation
Reports pK<sub>a</sub> of the conjugate acid NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> rather than the pH of the NH<sub>3</sub> solution itself
Confuses the pOH value of this weak base with the pH of an analogous weak acid situation, forgetting the final pH = 14 − pOH step
mixed_topics: Ionization of Weak Acids and Bases
Ionic Product of Water and the pH Scale

questions.question: A weak acid HA (K<sub>a</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>) at C = 0.2 M is mixed with its conjugate base at [A<sup>−</sup>] = 0.1 M (a common ion). Using [H<sup>+</sup>] ≈ K<sub>a</sub>[HA]/[A<sup>−</sup>], what is the resulting pH?
options: ≈ 4.74
≈ 4.44
≈ 9.56
≈ 2.44
questions.explanation: [H<sup>+</sup>] ≈ K<sub>a</sub> × [HA]/[A<sup>−</sup>] = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup> × (0.2/0.1) = 3.6 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M. pH = −log(3.6 × 10<sup>−5</sup>) ≈ 4.44.
questions.hint: This is the common-ion-suppressed-ionisation formula, essentially the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation in disguise — but here [HA] ≠ [A<sup>−</sup>], so don't assume pH = pK<sub>a</sub>.
distractor_logic: Assumes the 1:1-ratio result (pH = pK<sub>a</sub>) applies here, missing that [HA] is actually twice [A<sup>−</sup>] in this problem
Inverts the ratio inside the formula, effectively swapping which species is in excess
Uses the unsuppressed acid's own ionisation (ignoring the common ion entirely) instead of the common-ion-adjusted formula
mixed_topics: Ionization of Weak Acids and Bases

questions.question: For PCl<sub>5</sub>(g) ↔ PCl<sub>3</sub>(g) + Cl<sub>2</sub>(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 1.8 at 523 K. First find K<sub>p</sub> (R = 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>). Then, at an instant where P(PCl<sub>5</sub>) = 0.5 atm, P(PCl<sub>3</sub>) = 1.0 atm, and P(Cl<sub>2</sub>) = 1.0 atm, in which direction does the reaction proceed?
options: K<sub>p</sub> ≈ 0.042; Q<sub>p</sub> = 2.0, so the reverse reaction proceeds strongly
K<sub>p</sub> ≈ 77.3; Q<sub>p</sub> = 2.0, which is far less than K<sub>p</sub>, so the forward reaction proceeds
K<sub>p</sub> = 1.8 (same as K<sub>c</sub>); Q<sub>p</sub> = 2.0, so the reverse reaction proceeds slightly
K<sub>p</sub> ≈ 77.3; Q<sub>p</sub> = 2.0, which is far greater than K<sub>p</sub>, so the reverse reaction proceeds
questions.explanation: Δn = +1, so K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub>(RT) = 1.8 × (0.0821 × 523) ≈ 77.3. Q<sub>p</sub> = P(PCl<sub>3</sub>)P(Cl<sub>2</sub>)/P(PCl<sub>5</sub>) = (1.0 × 1.0)/0.5 = 2.0. Since Q<sub>p</sub> (2.0) is far less than K<sub>p</sub> (≈77.3), the system has proportionally too little product, so the forward reaction proceeds substantially.
questions.hint: Compute K<sub>p</sub> from K<sub>c</sub> FIRST — comparing Q<sub>p</sub> to the unconverted K<sub>c</sub> value instead would be comparing apples to oranges.
distractor_logic: Makes an error converting K<sub>c</sub> to K<sub>p</sub> (dividing instead of multiplying by RT), producing an implausibly small K<sub>p</sub>
Skips the K<sub>c</sub>-to-K<sub>p</sub> conversion, comparing Q<sub>p</sub> against K<sub>c</sub> directly, which is dimensionally inconsistent since Q<sub>p</sub> uses pressures
Correctly computes both values but reverses the comparison's directional conclusion

questions.question: For the heterogeneous equilibrium C(s) + H<sub>2</sub>O(g) ↔ CO(g) + H<sub>2</sub>(g), which of the following changes will actually shift the equilibrium position?
options: Decreasing the total pressure by increasing the container volume (favours the side with more gas moles)
Adding more solid carbon, C(s), while some already remains
Grinding the solid carbon into a finer powder
Removing some solid carbon, as long as some still remains
questions.explanation: Gas moles: 1 on the left (H<sub>2</sub>O) vs 2 on the right (CO + H<sub>2</sub>), so decreasing pressure (increasing volume) favours the side with more gas moles — the products — shifting equilibrium forward. The other three options change only the amount or physical form of the solid, which doesn't appear in K<sub>c</sub>/K<sub>p</sub> and has no effect on the equilibrium position, only (at most) on how quickly equilibrium is reached.
questions.hint: First ask whether a proposed change actually affects the concentration/pressure of a species that appears in the equilibrium expression at all — solids never do.
distractor_logic: Volume/pressure changes DO shift this equilibrium, since the gas moles differ on each side (1 vs 2) — this option wrongly claims no change occurs anywhere
Same reasoning error — removing solid (while some remains) still has no effect, for the same reason
Solids do not appear in the equilibrium expression, so changing the amount of C(s) (while some remains) has no effect on equilibrium position

questions.topic: Acids, Bases and the Lewis Concept
questions.question: BF<sub>3</sub> reacts with NH<sub>3</sub> to form the adduct F<sub>3</sub>B←NH<sub>3</sub>, with NH<sub>3</sub> donating its lone pair to boron. Which acid-base concept correctly classifies this reaction, and why can't a K<sub>a</sub> value (as used for weak acids like CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) be assigned to BF<sub>3</sub> in the usual sense?
options: K<sub>a</sub> does apply here, but with a different numeric definition specific to boron compounds

This is a Lewis acid-base reaction (BF<sub>3</sub> is the Lewis acid, NH<sub>3</sub> the Lewis base); K<sub>a</sub> specifically describes Bronsted-Lowry proton-transfer ionisation in water, which doesn't apply since no protons are transferred here
This is a Bronsted-Lowry reaction with BF<sub>3</sub> donating a proton, so K<sub>a</sub> should apply directly, just like for CH<sub>3</sub>COOH
This isn't an acid-base reaction at all, just an ordinary covalent bond formation unrelated to equilibrium concepts
questions.explanation: BF<sub>3</sub> has no proton to donate, so it cannot be a Bronsted-Lowry acid; instead it accepts an electron pair from NH<sub>3</sub>, making it a Lewis acid (and NH<sub>3</sub> the Lewis base, donating the pair). K<sub>a</sub> is specifically defined for the Bronsted-Lowry proton-transfer ionisation equilibrium in water (HA ↔ H<sup>+</sup> + A<sup>−</sup>), so it simply doesn't apply to a coordinate-bond forming Lewis acid-base reaction like this one.
questions.hint: Ask first: is a proton being transferred here, or an electron pair? That determines which acid-base framework — and which associated equilibrium constant — actually applies.
distractor_logic: Invents a nonexistent redefinition; K<sub>a</sub> as conventionally used simply has no meaning for this kind of coordinate-bond-forming reaction
Misidentifies which species donates what — BF<sub>3</sub> has no proton to donate, and this is not a Bronsted-Lowry proton-transfer reaction at all
This IS a genuine acid-base interaction under the (broader) Lewis definition, even though it involves no proton transfer
mixed_topics: Acids, Bases and the Lewis Concept
Ionization of Weak Acids and Bases

questions.question: A solution of pure 0.1 M CH<sub>3</sub>COONa is basic due to hydrolysis (pH ≈ 8.87), yet it does NOT behave as an effective buffer. Why not?
options: Its pH is not exactly 7, so it cannot be a buffer by definition
Sodium acetate is a strong electrolyte, and strong electrolytes can never participate in buffering
Hydrolysis reactions are irreversible, so no equilibrium exists to resist a pH change
It lacks a significant reservoir of undissociated CH<sub>3</sub>COOH; a buffer needs comparable amounts of BOTH a weak acid (or base) AND its conjugate partner, not just the hydrolysed salt alone
questions.explanation: A buffer's resistance to pH change comes from having both a weak acid/base AND its conjugate species present in comparable, appreciable amounts, so that added H<sup>+</sup> or OH<sup>−</sup> can be consumed by one or the other. Pure CH<sub>3</sub>COONa hydrolyses only slightly (h ≈ 7.5 × 10<sup>−5</sup>), producing only a tiny amount of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH — nowhere near enough to buffer against any real addition of acid or base.
questions.hint: Compare how MUCH CH<sub>3</sub>COOH is actually present in a hydrolysed salt solution to how much is present in a deliberately prepared 1:1 acid/salt buffer.
distractor_logic: A buffer can be maintained at many pH values, not just 7 — this is not the actual reason
Being a strong electrolyte (in terms of its own dissociation into Na<sup>+</sup> and CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>) doesn't by itself prevent participation in an acid-base equilibrium
Hydrolysis is very much an equilibrium (reversible) process, described by a hydrolysis constant K<sub>h</sub>, just like any other weak-electrolyte equilibrium

questions.question: A solution contains both 0.01 M Ag<sup>+</sup> and 0.01 M Pb<sup>2+</sup>. K<sub>sp</sub>(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10<sup>−10</sup> and K<sub>sp</sub>(PbCl<sub>2</sub>) = 1.7 × 10<sup>−5</sup>. If Cl<sup>−</sup> is added slowly, which salt precipitates first?
options: Neither precipitates, since Cl<sup>−</sup> is a common ion for both and would suppress both equilibria equally
AgCl, since it requires a much lower [Cl<sup>−</sup>] to reach its K<sub>sp</sub> ([Cl<sup>−</sup>] ≈ 1.8 × 10<sup>−8</sup> M for AgCl, versus ≈ 0.041 M for PbCl<sub>2</sub>)
Both precipitate simultaneously, since both cations are present at the same 0.01 M concentration
PbCl<sub>2</sub>, since Pb<sup>2+</sup> is a larger, heavier ion
questions.explanation: For AgCl, precipitation begins when [Cl<sup>−</sup>] = K<sub>sp</sub>/[Ag<sup>+</sup>] = 1.8 × 10<sup>−10</sup>/0.01 = 1.8 × 10<sup>−8</sup> M. For PbCl<sub>2</sub> (AB<sub>2</sub>-type), [Cl<sup>−</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = K<sub>sp</sub>/[Pb<sup>2+</sup>] = 1.7 × 10<sup>−5</sup>/0.01 = 1.7 × 10<sup>−3</sup>, so [Cl<sup>−</sup>] ≈ 0.041 M. Since AgCl needs vastly less Cl<sup>−</sup> to start precipitating, it precipitates first — this is the basis of selective precipitation / qualitative salt analysis.
questions.hint: Compute the [Cl<sup>−</sup>] needed to just reach K<sub>sp</sub> for EACH salt separately, then compare which threshold is reached first as Cl<sup>−</sup> is added gradually.
distractor_logic: A shared (common) ion suppresses a salt's OWN solubility once introduced, but here it is the very reagent being added to trigger, not suppress, precipitation — the two salts still have very different thresholds
Ignores that the two salts have very different K<sub>sp</sub> values and different stoichiometries, so their thresholds for precipitation are very different
Uses an irrelevant physical property (ion mass/size) instead of the actual K<sub>sp</sub>-based threshold comparison

questions.topic: Degree of Dissociation and Ostwald's Dilution Law
questions.question: The Ostwald approximation α ≈ √(K<sub>a</sub>/C) and the K<sub>sp</sub>-to-solubility formula s = √K<sub>sp</sub> (for an AB-type salt) both involve taking a square root of a ratio or constant. What assumption do these two calculations share?
options: Both assume the amount reacted/dissolved (α or s) is small enough that the initial concentration term in the denominator of the equilibrium expression is not significantly changed by it
Both are only valid for gas-phase equilibria
Both require the presence of a common ion to be valid
Both assume the reaction goes to 100% completion
questions.explanation: In the Ostwald approximation, (1−α) is approximated as 1 because α is small — this is valid for dilute weak electrolytes. Similarly, for K<sub>sp</sub> = s<sup>2</sup>, the underlying assumption is that dissolution starting from pure solid doesn't require subtracting anything from an initial concentration (there is no competing initial concentration to begin with, which is why this particular case needs no approximation at all) — but more generally, whenever a common ion or comparable background concentration IS present in either type of problem, the 'small quantity' shortcut can break down and the full expression must be used, just as in the exact α quadratic.
questions.hint: Think about why each formula is only an approximation (or, for the simplest AB-Ksp case, an exact simplification) rather than the full equilibrium expression — what's being neglected or simplified?
distractor_logic: Both are general equilibrium concepts, equally applicable in solution (as used throughout this chapter for ionic equilibria), not restricted to gases
Neither requires a common ion to be present — indeed, both are usually first introduced for the simplest case with NO common ion present
Neither calculation assumes complete reaction; both describe genuinely partial, equilibrium processes (that's the entire point of K<sub>a</sub> and K<sub>sp</sub> both being finite, not infinite)
mixed_topics: Degree of Dissociation and Ostwald's Dilution Law

questions.question: When a stress (such as adding more reactant) is applied to a system at equilibrium, Le Chatelier's principle predicts a shift that partially counteracts the stress. How does the reaction quotient Q explain WHY this shift happens, in quantitative terms?
options: Adding reactant instantly lowers Q below K (since Q's denominator grows), and since Q < K signals 'not enough product yet', the forward reaction proceeds until Q rises back to equal K
Q and K are unrelated ideas; Le Chatelier's principle needs no reference to Q to be justified
Adding reactant doesn't change Q at all, since Q depends only on products
Adding reactant instantly raises Q above K, forcing the reverse reaction to dominate
questions.explanation: Q shares the same mathematical form as K, and reactant concentrations sit in Q's denominator. Suddenly adding more reactant makes that denominator larger, dropping Q below the (unchanged) K value. Since Q < K means 'proportionally too few products for this reaction to be at rest', the system responds by shifting forward — precisely the shift Le Chatelier's principle predicts — until Q climbs back up to equal K at the new equilibrium.
questions.hint: Q contains BOTH reactants and products in its expression — trace exactly how adding more reactant changes the ratio, then connect that to the Q-versus-K comparison rule.
distractor_logic: This is exactly the deeper, quantitative justification for Le Chatelier's principle, not an unrelated idea
Q depends on both reactant AND product concentrations by definition (it uses the same expression as K), so adding reactant absolutely does change Q
Reverses which side of the Q < K / Q > K comparison corresponds to more reactant being added

questions.question: For the physical equilibrium H<sub>2</sub>O(l) ↔ H<sub>2</sub>O(g), raising the temperature increases the equilibrium vapour pressure. Applying Le Chatelier-style reasoning (treating vaporisation as an endothermic process, since heat must be supplied to vaporise a liquid), why does this make sense?
options: Vapour pressure increases with temperature purely due to increased container volume, unrelated to equilibrium shifting
Le Chatelier's principle applies only to chemical reactions, not physical equilibria, so this trend needs a completely separate explanation
Heat behaves like a 'product', so raising temperature should actually decrease the vapour pressure

Heat behaves like a 'reactant' for the endothermic vaporisation process, so adding heat (raising temperature) shifts the physical equilibrium toward more vapour, raising the equilibrium vapour pressure
questions.explanation: Vaporisation absorbs heat (it's endothermic), so in Le Chatelier terms heat acts like a reactant being consumed by the forward (liquid→gas) process. Supplying more heat (raising T) is exactly the kind of stress that pushes such an equilibrium further toward the vapour side, which is observed directly as a higher equilibrium vapour pressure — Le Chatelier's principle extends naturally to physical equilibria, not just chemical reactions.
questions.hint: Decide whether heat is being absorbed or released by the liquid-to-vapour direction, then apply the same heat-as-reactant-or-product logic used for chemical equilibria.
distractor_logic: The container volume is not what's driving this specific trend; it's the shift in the liquid-vapour equilibrium itself in response to temperature, matching real observed data on vapour pressure vs T
Le Chatelier's principle is general and applies to ANY equilibrium — chemical or physical — that responds to changes in concentration, pressure, or temperature
Reverses which side heat belongs to for this endothermic physical process

questions.topic: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constant
questions.question: Pure solids and liquids are omitted from K<sub>c</sub> because their concentration is essentially constant. How does this same reasoning carry over to writing K<sub>p</sub> for a heterogeneous equilibrium like CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) ↔ CaO(s) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g)?
options: K<sub>p</sub> cannot be defined at all for heterogeneous equilibria, only K<sub>c</sub> can
K<sub>p</sub> for this reaction equals P(CaO)/P(CaCO<sub>3</sub>), by direct analogy with the wrong K<sub>c</sub> expression
Solids have no meaningful 'partial pressure' either, so K<sub>p</sub> for this reaction is written using only the gas — K<sub>p</sub> = P(CO<sub>2</sub>)
K<sub>p</sub> must still include solids, expressed as their vapour pressure
questions.explanation: The same logic that excludes solids from K<sub>c</sub> (their molar concentration is a fixed material property, not a variable) applies directly to K<sub>p</sub>: solids simply don't have a meaningful 'partial pressure' that varies with the reaction's progress, so they're excluded there too, leaving K<sub>p</sub> = P(CO<sub>2</sub>) for this particular reaction.
questions.hint: Ask the same question for K<sub>p</sub> as for K<sub>c</sub>: does this species' amount actually change in a way that affects a measurable pressure/concentration term?
distractor_logic: K<sub>p</sub> is perfectly well defined for heterogeneous equilibria — it's simply restricted to the gas-phase species, exactly as demonstrated correctly in the intended answer
Wrongly copies over the very same mistaken K<sub>c</sub> expression pattern that including solids would produce, rather than correctly restricting to the gas species
Solids under normal conditions do not have an appreciable, reaction-relevant vapour pressure that would belong in this expression
mixed_topics: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constant

questions.topic: Ionic Product of Water and the pH Scale
questions.question: A 1 L solution of 0.01 M HCl (pH = 2) is diluted 10-fold to 0.001 M (pH = 3) — a full pH unit change. In contrast, a 1 L acetic acid/acetate buffer at pH 4.74 changes by only a small fraction of a pH unit when diluted the same 10-fold. Why does the buffer resist the change so much more effectively?
options: Strong acids are simply immune to any pH change upon dilution, so the pH 2 → 3 shift described here is not physically real
Buffers are only stable in extremely small dilutions, and 10-fold dilution should have broken this buffer's resistance too

Diluting the buffer changes [acid] and [salt] by the same factor, so their RATIO (which sets the pH via pH = pK<sub>a</sub> + log(ratio)) stays almost unchanged, whereas diluting a strong acid directly and proportionally changes [H<sup>+</sup>] itself
The buffer's K<sub>a</sub> value itself changes upon dilution to compensate
questions.explanation: For a strong acid, [H<sup>+</sup>] IS the concentration itself, so any dilution directly and proportionally lowers [H<sup>+</sup>], moving pH by a full unit per 10-fold dilution. For a buffer, pH depends on the RATIO [salt]/[acid] via Henderson-Hasselbalch — and since dilution reduces both the salt and acid concentrations by the same factor, their ratio (and hence the pH) barely changes, which is precisely the buffer's defining resistance property.
questions.hint: Focus on what pH actually depends on in each case: an absolute concentration for the strong acid, versus a RATIO of two concentrations for the buffer.
distractor_logic: The pH 2 → 3 shift for a strong acid upon 10-fold dilution is a completely standard, real result (pH = −log[H<sup>+</sup>] applied directly)
This is exactly backwards — buffers resist pH change over a wide range of moderate dilutions; only very extreme dilution eventually breaks a buffer's capacity
K<sub>a</sub> is a genuine constant at fixed temperature; it does not change with dilution or concentration
mixed_topics: Ionic Product of Water and the pH Scale

questions.question: The common ion effect (e.g. adding CH<sub>3</sub>COONa to suppress CH<sub>3</sub>COOH's ionisation) is often introduced as its own separate idea, but it can also be seen as a specific case of a more general principle covered earlier in this chapter. Which principle, and how?
options: The law of mass action — because K<sub>a</sub> changes when a common ion is added
The Kp-Kc relationship — because both involve a constant multiplied by a concentration term

Le Chatelier's principle — adding a common ion is simply a 'stress' in the form of increased product concentration, which shifts the ionisation equilibrium backward exactly as any concentration stress would
Ostwald's dilution law — because adding a common ion is mathematically identical to dilution
questions.explanation: Adding a common ion is exactly the 'increase in product concentration' stress described generally under Le Chatelier's principle; the equilibrium (here, HA ↔ H<sup>+</sup> + A<sup>−</sup>) responds by shifting backward to partially counteract the added A<sup>−</sup>, which IS the suppression of ionisation observed. The common ion effect is simply Le Chatelier's principle applied specifically to a shared-ion equilibrium.
questions.hint: Ask what KIND of stress 'adding a common ion' represents in the general concentration/pressure/temperature categorisation used by Le Chatelier's principle.
distractor_logic: K<sub>a</sub> never changes with concentration; only the equilibrium POSITION (extent of ionisation) shifts, and K<sub>a</sub> itself remains fixed at constant temperature
The Kp-Kc relationship is a mathematical conversion tool, unrelated to the qualitative direction-of-shift reasoning involved in the common ion effect
Dilution and common ion addition have OPPOSITE effects on α (dilution increases it, common ion addition decreases it), so they are not the same phenomenon

questions.question: CaCO<sub>3</sub> is only sparingly soluble in pure water (governed by its K<sub>sp</sub>), but dissolves much more readily in dilute acid. Using ideas from both solubility equilibria and hydrolysis/weak-acid behaviour, why does adding acid increase CaCO<sub>3</sub>'s solubility?
options: H<sup>+</sup> from the acid reacts with the CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> ion (a species that also hydrolyses, being the conjugate base of the weak acid HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>), removing it from solution and, by Le Chatelier's principle applied to the K<sub>sp</sub> equilibrium, pulling more CaCO<sub>3</sub> into solution to replace it
K<sub>sp</sub> of CaCO<sub>3</sub> itself becomes larger in the presence of acid
This has nothing to do with CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> at all — acid instead reacts directly with solid Ca<sup>2+</sup> ions in the lattice
Acid has no chemical effect on CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>; CaCO<sub>3</sub> dissolves more only because acidic solutions are generally better solvents for all ionic solids
questions.explanation: CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> is a Bronsted-Lowry base (conjugate base of the weak acid HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>) and reacts with added H<sup>+</sup>: CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> → HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> (and further to H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>/CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O). This consumes CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> from the K<sub>sp</sub> equilibrium CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) ↔ Ca<sup>2+</sup> + CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>, and by Le Chatelier's principle, removing a product drives more solid to dissolve, replacing the consumed ion — increasing overall solubility.
questions.hint: Identify which ion of the sparingly soluble salt is itself a weak base capable of reacting further with added H<sup>+</sup>, then connect that consumption back to the K<sub>sp</sub> equilibrium via Le Chatelier's principle.
distractor_logic: K<sub>sp</sub> doesn't change with the presence of acid; the shift is due to consumption of CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> by a separate, coupled acid-base reaction
Ca<sup>2+</sup> itself doesn't react with H<sup>+</sup>; it's specifically CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>, the basic anion, that is consumed

K<sub>sp</sub> is a true equilibrium constant, fixed at a given temperature; it doesn't change simply because a different reagent (acid) happens to be present — what changes is that a coupled reaction removes one of the ions

questions.topic: Ionization of Weak Acids and Bases
questions.question: Propionic acid (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH) has K<sub>a</sub> = 1.3 × 10<sup>−5</sup>. What is the hydrolysis constant K<sub>h</sub> of its conjugate base, the propionate ion, and is this hydrolysis significant compared to acetate's (K<sub>h</sub> ≈ 5.6 × 10<sup>−10</sup>)?
options: K<sub>h</sub> cannot be found without knowing the exact salt concentration

K<sub>h</sub> = K<sub>w</sub>/K<sub>a</sub> ≈ 7.7 × 10<sup>−10</sup>, of a very similar (small) order of magnitude to acetate's K<sub>h</sub>, since propionic acid and acetic acid have similar K<sub>a</sub> values
K<sub>h</sub> = K<sub>a</sub>/K<sub>w</sub> ≈ 1.3 × 10<sup>9</sup>, vastly larger than acetate's
K<sub>h</sub> = K<sub>a</sub> directly, since K<sub>h</sub> and K<sub>a</sub> describe the same reaction
questions.explanation: K<sub>h</sub> = K<sub>w</sub>/K<sub>a</sub> = (1.0 × 10<sup>−14</sup>)/(1.3 × 10<sup>−5</sup>) ≈ 7.7 × 10<sup>−10</sup>. Since propionic acid's K<sub>a</sub> is of the same order of magnitude as acetic acid's (1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>), its conjugate base's K<sub>h</sub> is similarly small — both propionate and acetate are only weakly basic/hydrolysed in water, consistent with both being conjugate bases of comparably weak acids.
questions.hint: Use K<sub>h</sub> = K<sub>w</sub>/K<sub>a</sub> exactly as for acetate, then compare the resulting order of magnitude rather than the exact value.
distractor_logic: K<sub>h</sub> is an equilibrium constant, fixed by K<sub>w</sub> and K<sub>a</sub> alone at a given temperature — it does not require knowing the salt's actual concentration to calculate (though the resulting degree of hydrolysis h would)
Inverts the K<sub>h</sub>=K<sub>w</sub>/K<sub>a</sub> relationship, producing a nonsensical value much larger than 1
Confuses K<sub>h</sub> (hydrolysis constant of the conjugate base) with K<sub>a</sub> (ionisation constant of the parent acid) — these describe two different, though related, equilibria

questions.question: For the heterogeneous equilibrium 2NaHCO<sub>3</sub>(s) ↔ Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>(s) + H<sub>2</sub>O(g) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g), what is K<sub>p</sub>, and what is Δn for converting it to K<sub>c</sub>?
options: K<sub>p</sub> cannot be written since there are no gaseous reactants at all
K<sub>p</sub> = P(H<sub>2</sub>O) × P(CO<sub>2</sub>)/P(NaHCO<sub>3</sub>)<sup>2</sup>; Δn = 0
K<sub>p</sub> = P(H<sub>2</sub>O) × P(CO<sub>2</sub>); Δn = +2 (two moles of gas appear from zero moles of gaseous reactant)
K<sub>p</sub> = P(Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>)/P(NaHCO<sub>3</sub>)<sup>2</sup>; Δn = −2
questions.explanation: Only the gas-phase species (H<sub>2</sub>O and CO<sub>2</sub>) enter K<sub>p</sub>, giving K<sub>p</sub> = P(H<sub>2</sub>O) × P(CO<sub>2</sub>); the solids NaHCO<sub>3</sub> and Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> are omitted exactly as in any other heterogeneous equilibrium. Since there are zero moles of gaseous reactant and 2 moles of gaseous product, Δn = 2 − 0 = +2.
questions.hint: First strip out the solids to get the K<sub>p</sub> expression, then count ONLY the gas-phase moles on each side to find Δn — the solids never contribute to Δn either.
distractor_logic: K<sub>p</sub> is perfectly definable here — heterogeneous equilibria are handled by simply restricting the K<sub>p</sub> expression to gas-phase species, even when only products (and no reactants) are gases
Wrongly includes the solid NaHCO<sub>3</sub> in the K<sub>p</sub> expression and then miscounts Δn as if reactant gas moles existed
Wrongly includes only some solids and gets the expression form backwards, and computes Δn as if moles decreased rather than increased

questions.topic: Degree of Dissociation and Ostwald's Dilution Law
questions.question: 0.1 M CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (K<sub>a</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>) alone has α ≈ 0.0134. If enough CH<sub>3</sub>COONa is added to make [CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>] = 0.1 M as well, what is the NEW α of the acetic acid (as a fraction of the original 0.1 M acid, not a fresh quantity), using [H<sup>+</sup>] ≈ K<sub>a</sub>[acid]/[salt] and α = [H<sup>+</sup>]/C?
options: α ≈ 1.8 × 10<sup>−4</sup> (0.018%), about 75 times smaller than the unsuppressed α of 0.0134
α ≈ 1.0 (100%), since the extra ions push the reaction to completion
α ≈ 0.0134, unchanged, since α only depends on K<sub>a</sub> and C, not on other ions present
α ≈ 0.1, equal to the salt's concentration
questions.explanation: [H<sup>+</sup>] ≈ K<sub>a</sub>[acid]/[salt] = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup> × (0.1/0.1) = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M. α = [H<sup>+</sup>]/C = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>/0.1 = 1.8 × 10<sup>−4</sup>, roughly 75 times smaller than the 0.0134 found without the common ion — a direct, quantitative demonstration of the common ion effect suppressing α, using the same α = [H<sup>+</sup>]/C definition introduced for plain weak-acid ionisation.
questions.hint: Find [H<sup>+</sup>] using the common-ion-suppressed formula first, THEN divide by C to get α — the definition of α itself doesn't change, only the [H<sup>+</sup>] that goes into it.
distractor_logic: Grossly overstates the suppression's reverse — a common ion suppresses ionisation, it does not drive it toward completion
Ignores the common ion's suppressing effect on [H<sup>+</sup>], and hence on α, entirely
Confuses α (a fraction between 0 and 1) with the salt's own concentration, an unrelated number
mixed_topics: Degree of Dissociation and Ostwald's Dilution Law

questions.question: Explain, in Le Chatelier terms, why adding a small amount of strong acid (H<sup>+</sup>) to an acetate buffer (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH/CH<sub>3</sub>COONa) causes only a small pH change rather than a large one.
options: The buffer simply neutralises all added acid completely, keeping [H<sup>+</sup>] at exactly zero

The added H<sup>+</sup> is consumed by the conjugate base CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> (shifting CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>COOH), converting most of the added strong acid into a comparatively small increase in the weak, only-partially-ionised acid, rather than leaving it as free H<sup>+</sup> in solution
K<sub>a</sub> of acetic acid decreases automatically when acid is added, offsetting the change
The buffer has no real mechanism for resisting pH change; the small observed change is coincidental
questions.explanation: The conjugate base present in the buffer (CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>) reacts with most of the added H<sup>+</sup>, converting it into undissociated CH<sub>3</sub>COOH. Since CH<sub>3</sub>COOH itself only weakly re-ionises, very little of that H<sup>+</sup> remains free in solution, so [H<sup>+</sup>] — and hence pH — barely moves compared to what would happen if the same acid were added to unbuffered water.
questions.hint: Track WHERE the added H<sup>+</sup> actually goes — does it stay as free H<sup>+</sup>, or does it get captured by another species already present in the buffer?
distractor_logic: Overstates the effect; a buffer resists but does not completely eliminate pH change — this is why the buffer's pH does shift slightly (as seen in the equimolar-buffer-plus-NaOH example elsewhere in this chapter)
K<sub>a</sub> is a genuine constant at fixed temperature and does not change when acid or base is added
The buffer's resistance is a direct, well-understood consequence of the conjugate acid-base equilibrium present, not a coincidence

questions.question: Using the general law of mass action (products over reactants, with stoichiometric coefficients as exponents, solid omitted), what is the correct K<sub>sp</sub> expression for calcium phosphate, Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>(s) ↔ 3Ca<sup>2+</sup> + 2PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>?
options: K<sub>sp</sub> = [Ca<sup>2+</sup>]<sup>2</sup>[PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>]<sup>3</sup>
K<sub>sp</sub> = [Ca<sup>2+</sup>][PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>]
K<sub>sp</sub> = [Ca<sup>2+</sup>]<sup>3</sup>[PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>]<sup>2</sup>
K<sub>sp</sub> = 3[Ca<sup>2+</sup>] + 2[PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>]
questions.explanation: Applying the general law of mass action exactly as for any other K<sub>sp</sub>: each ion's concentration is raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient in the dissolution equation. Here that gives K<sub>sp</sub> = [Ca<sup>2+</sup>]<sup>3</sup>[PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>]<sup>2</sup>, matching the 3 and 2 coefficients shown in the dissolution equation — this generalises the same AB, AB<sub>2</sub>, and A<sub>2</sub>B patterns already seen to a more complex A<sub>3</sub>B<sub>2</sub>-type salt.
questions.hint: Match each ion's exponent directly to its own coefficient from the balanced dissolution equation, exactly as with any K<sub>c</sub> expression.
distractor_logic: Swaps the exponents between the two ions, assigning Ca<sup>2+</sup> the power that actually belongs to PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup> and vice versa
Wrongly treats this like a simple 1:1 AB-type salt, ignoring the 3 and 2 coefficients entirely
Adds the concentrations instead of taking their product with the correct powers, the same generic error as writing any K<sub>c</sub>/K<sub>sp</sub> expression incorrectly
mixed_topics: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constant

questions.topic: Ionic Product of Water and the pH Scale
questions.question: A solution is 0.1 M in both CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (K<sub>a</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>) and HCOOH, formic acid (K<sub>a</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−4</sup>, ten times larger). Which acid dominates in determining the solution's [H<sup>+</sup>], and what is the approximate pH?
options: The pH cannot be determined when two different weak acids are present together
Both contribute exactly equally, so [H<sup>+</sup>] is the simple sum of each acid's individual [H<sup>+</sup>], doubling the concentration
Acetic acid dominates, since it was listed first; pH ≈ 2.87
Formic acid dominates (its much larger K<sub>a</sub> means it ionises far more); treating it alone, [H<sup>+</sup>] ≈ √(1.8 × 10<sup>−4</sup> × 0.1) ≈ 4.2 × 10<sup>−3</sup> M, giving pH ≈ 2.37
questions.explanation: With a tenfold larger K<sub>a</sub>, formic acid ionises to a much greater extent and supplies far more H<sup>+</sup> than acetic acid does at the same concentration; the acetic acid's own ionisation is further suppressed by the H<sup>+</sup> that formic acid already provides (a common ion effect between the two acids). To a good approximation, treating formic acid alone: [H<sup>+</sup>] ≈ √(K<sub>a</sub>C) = √(1.8 × 10<sup>−4</sup> × 0.1) ≈ 4.2 × 10<sup>−3</sup> M, so pH ≈ 2.37 — noticeably lower (more acidic) than acetic acid alone would give (pH ≈ 2.87).
questions.hint: Compare the two K<sub>a</sub> values first — the stronger acid (larger K<sub>a</sub>) dominates the solution's [H<sup>+</sup>], with the weaker acid's own contribution further suppressed by a common ion (H<sup>+</sup>) effect.
distractor_logic: The dominant-acid approximation (using whichever K<sub>a</sub> is much larger) handles exactly this kind of mixed weak-acid system at the NCERT level

Simply adding independently-calculated [H<sup>+</sup>] values double-counts the suppression each acid exerts on the other via the shared H<sup>+</sup> common ion, overestimating the true combined [H<sup>+</sup>]
The listing order in the question has no bearing on which acid actually dominates chemically

questions.question: For N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(g) ↔ 2NO<sub>2</sub>(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 4.63 × 10<sup>−3</sup> at 298 K. First find K<sub>p</sub> (R = 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>). Then, given P(N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) = 0.5 atm and P(NO<sub>2</sub>) = 0.1 atm at some instant, determine the direction of reaction using Q<sub>p</sub>.
options: K<sub>p</sub> ≈ 0.113; Q<sub>p</sub> = (0.1)<sup>2</sup>/0.5 = 0.02, which is less than K<sub>p</sub>, so the forward reaction proceeds
K<sub>p</sub> ≈ 0.113; Q<sub>p</sub> = 0.02, which is greater than K<sub>p</sub>, so the reverse reaction proceeds
K<sub>p</sub> ≈ 1.89 × 10<sup>−4</sup>; Q<sub>p</sub> = 0.02, so forward reaction proceeds strongly
K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub> = 4.63 × 10<sup>−3</sup>; Q<sub>p</sub> = 0.02, so reverse reaction proceeds
questions.explanation: Δn = +1, so K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub>(RT) = 4.63 × 10<sup>−3</sup> × (0.0821 × 298) ≈ 0.113. Q<sub>p</sub> = P(NO<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup>/P(N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) = (0.1)<sup>2</sup>/0.5 = 0.01/0.5 = 0.02. Since Q<sub>p</sub> (0.02) is less than K<sub>p</sub> (≈0.113), the forward reaction proceeds, producing more NO<sub>2</sub>.
questions.hint: Convert K<sub>c</sub> to K<sub>p</sub> BEFORE comparing to Q<sub>p</sub>, since Q<sub>p</sub> is built from pressures, not concentrations.
distractor_logic: Correctly computes both values but reverses the direction implied by Q<sub>p</sub> < K<sub>p</sub>
Makes an error in the K<sub>c</sub>-to-K<sub>p</sub> conversion (dividing by (RT) instead of multiplying), producing a K<sub>p</sub> smaller than K<sub>c</sub> despite Δn being positive

Skips the necessary K<sub>c</sub>-to-K<sub>p</sub> conversion, comparing Q<sub>p</sub> (a pressure-based quantity) directly against K<sub>c</sub> (a concentration-based quantity) as though they were the same

questions.question: For NH<sub>4</sub>HS(s) ↔ NH<sub>3</sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>S(g) in a sealed vessel, which of the following would shift the equilibrium, and which would not?
options: Neither change has any effect, since this is a heterogeneous equilibrium and heterogeneous equilibria never respond to any stress
Adding more solid NH<sub>4</sub>HS WOULD shift it forward (producing more gas), while adding NH<sub>3</sub>(g) would NOT
Both adding NH<sub>3</sub>(g) and adding more solid NH<sub>4</sub>HS would shift the equilibrium equally
Adding extra NH<sub>3</sub>(g) WOULD shift it (reverse, forming more solid); adding more solid NH<sub>4</sub>HS (with some already present) would NOT shift it
questions.explanation: NH<sub>3</sub>(g) is a gas-phase species that DOES appear in the equilibrium expression (K<sub>p</sub> = P(NH<sub>3</sub>)×P(H<sub>2</sub>S)), so adding more of it is a genuine concentration stress that shifts equilibrium in reverse (Le Chatelier). The solid NH<sub>4</sub>HS, however, doesn't appear in the equilibrium expression at all (as with any pure solid), so adding more of it (while some remains) has no effect on the equilibrium position — this correctly distinguishes which species matter using both the heterogeneous-equilibrium rule and Le Chatelier's principle together.
questions.hint: For each proposed change, first ask 'does this species even appear in the equilibrium expression?' before applying Le Chatelier's principle to it.
distractor_logic: Heterogeneous equilibria absolutely can and do respond to changes in the concentration/pressure of species that DO appear in their equilibrium expression (like the gases here) — it's only the omitted solid/liquid species that don't matter
Reverses which change matters — it's the gas addition that shifts equilibrium, not the solid addition
Wrongly treats the solid as equally capable of shifting equilibrium as the gas, ignoring the heterogeneous-equilibrium rule that solids are omitted from K

questions.topic: Acids, Bases and the Lewis Concept
questions.question: HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> (bicarbonate) is amphoteric: it can act as a Bronsted-Lowry acid (donating a proton to become CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>) or as a base (accepting a proton to become H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>). If HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> is reacted with a strong base like NaOH, which role does it play, and what does this predict about the pH direction of that reaction?
options: It acts as neither an acid nor a base here, remaining a completely inert spectator ion

It acts as an acid (donating a proton to OH<sup>−</sup>, forming water and CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>); consuming the added strong base this way means the pH rises by less than it would if no such reaction occurred
It cannot react with NaOH at all, since both are already basic species
It acts as a base (accepting a proton), which would require NaOH to supply a proton — impossible for a strong base
questions.explanation: Faced with the strong base OH<sup>−</sup> (a proton acceptor), HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> plays the role of proton DONOR — i.e. a Bronsted-Lowry acid — reacting as HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> + OH<sup>−</sup> → CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O. Because some of the added OH<sup>−</sup> is consumed by this reaction (rather than remaining free in solution), the resulting pH rise is moderated compared to adding the same NaOH to pure water — an early illustration of how amphoteric/buffering species can dampen pH swings.
questions.hint: A species facing a strong base can only act as a proton donor (acid) toward it, since a strong base is itself already the stronger proton acceptor — check which behaviour is chemically possible here.
distractor_logic: It participates directly and specifically as the acidic partner in this proton-transfer reaction, not as an inert spectator
HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>'s amphoteric nature specifically means it CAN react with both acids and bases, including strong ones like NaOH
Reverses HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>'s role — facing OH<sup>−</sup> (a proton acceptor), it cannot also act as a proton acceptor in the same reaction; a strong base cannot itself donate a proton

questions.question: For PCl<sub>5</sub>(g) ↔ PCl<sub>3</sub>(g) + Cl<sub>2</sub>(g), K<sub>p</sub> = 2.0 at 600 K. First convert to K<sub>c</sub> (R = 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>), then find α for 1.0 mol PCl<sub>5</sub> placed in a 1 L flask.
options: K<sub>c</sub> ≈ 2.0; α ≈ 0.82 (82%)
K<sub>c</sub> ≈ 0.0406; α ≈ 0.182 (18.2%)
K<sub>c</sub> ≈ 98.5; α ≈ 0.90 (90%)
K<sub>c</sub> ≈ 0.0406; α ≈ 0.50 (50%)
questions.explanation: Δn = +1, so K<sub>c</sub> = K<sub>p</sub>/(RT) = 2.0/(0.0821 × 600) = 2.0/49.26 ≈ 0.0406. With C<sub>0</sub> = 1.0 M: 1.0α<sup>2</sup> + 0.0406α − 0.0406 = 0. Solving gives α ≈ 0.182, i.e. about 18.2%.
questions.hint: Same two-step pattern as before: strip (RT) out of K<sub>p</sub> first to get K<sub>c</sub>, then solve the α quadratic using that K<sub>c</sub> and the given C<sub>0</sub>.
distractor_logic: Skips the conversion, mistakenly using K<sub>p</sub> directly as K<sub>c</sub> in the α quadratic
Multiplies by (RT) instead of dividing (treats Δn as −1), inflating K<sub>c</sub> and then α well beyond what the actual numbers support
Uses the small-α approximation instead of solving the full quadratic, which is not valid enough here to match any of the more precise listed options

questions.question: Ammonium acetate (CH<sub>3</sub>COONH<sub>4</sub>) is added to a solution that already contains some NH<sub>4</sub>Cl. Which ion from the added salt is a 'common ion' with the hydrolysis equilibrium of the NH<sub>4</sub>Cl already present, and what effect does it have?
options: Neither ion is common to the NH<sub>4</sub>Cl hydrolysis equilibrium, so there is no effect
Both ions together completely reverse the hydrolysis, making the solution strongly basic

NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> is common to both; the extra NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> suppresses the hydrolysis of the original NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O ↔ NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>), by the same Le-Chatelier logic as any other common ion effect
CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> is common to both, and it promotes the hydrolysis of NH<sub>4</sub>Cl
questions.explanation: NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> is a product species in NH<sub>4</sub>Cl's own hydrolysis equilibrium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O ↔ NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>) and is also supplied by the added CH<sub>3</sub>COONH<sub>4</sub>. This extra common NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> shifts that hydrolysis equilibrium backward, suppressing it — exactly the same Le Chatelier-based reasoning used for common ion suppression of ordinary weak-acid or weak-base ionisation, now applied to a hydrolysis equilibrium instead.
questions.hint: Hydrolysis is itself an equilibrium, so the same common-ion logic used for ionisation equilibria applies — just identify which ion is shared between the two salts here.
distractor_logic: Both ions ARE relevant to some equilibrium in this mixed solution (acetate has its own hydrolysis too), but the question specifically asks about the NH<sub>4</sub>Cl hydrolysis, which shares NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, not acetate

The addition of a common ion suppresses, rather than reverses outright, the specific equilibrium it's common to — the solution's overall character depends on the balance of both salts' hydrolysis, not a single dramatic reversal
Misidentifies which ion is actually shared between the two salts and the hydrolysis reaction in question

questions.question: A carbonate mineral like CaCO<sub>3</sub> is more soluble in an acidic buffer (say, pH 5) than in a neutral or basic buffer (say, pH 9), because CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> reacts with H<sup>+</sup>. Why does buffering the solution (rather than letting pH drift) matter for making a clean, reproducible solubility measurement?
options: Buffers prevent CaCO<sub>3</sub> from dissolving at all, so no reaction with H<sup>+</sup> actually occurs
A buffer converts CaCO<sub>3</sub> into a completely different, non-ionic compound
Buffering has no real effect on this system; K<sub>sp</sub> alone determines solubility regardless of pH

A buffer holds [H<sup>+</sup>] essentially fixed even as CaCO<sub>3</sub> dissolves and consumes some H<sup>+</sup>, so the CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>-consuming reaction proceeds consistently at a known, stable pH rather than the solution's acidity drifting upward as dissolution proceeds
questions.explanation: As CaCO<sub>3</sub> dissolves and its CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> reacts with H<sup>+</sup>, an unbuffered solution's pH would drift upward (becoming less acidic) as H<sup>+</sup> is consumed, slowing and complicating the process. A buffer resists this by replenishing consumed H<sup>+</sup> (or absorbing released OH<sup>−</sup>-equivalent effects) from its own conjugate acid/base reservoir, keeping pH essentially fixed so the coupled K<sub>sp</sub>/hydrolysis system reaches a well-defined, reproducible equilibrium rather than a constantly shifting one.
questions.hint: Think about what would happen to the solution's pH DURING dissolution if it were NOT buffered, and how that changing pH would affect the ongoing CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>-H<sup>+</sup> reaction.
distractor_logic: This describes the opposite of buffering's actual purpose here — the buffer specifically allows (and stabilises the conditions for) the enhanced dissolution to proceed cleanly, not prevents it
Buffering doesn't chemically transform CaCO<sub>3</sub>; it simply stabilises the solution's pH during the same dissolution and coupled acid-base reactions
This directly contradicts the premise that pH strongly affects CaCO<sub>3</sub> solubility via the coupled hydrolysis/Ksp equilibria discussed

questions.topic: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constant
questions.question: For the heterogeneous equilibrium Ag<sub>2</sub>O(s) + 2HNO<sub>3</sub>(aq) ↔ 2AgNO<sub>3</sub>(aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O(l) (all in aqueous solution except the solid), which species are correctly included when writing the reaction quotient Q for this system?
options: None of the species, since Q cannot be written for reactions involving a solid
Only Ag<sub>2</sub>O(s) and H<sub>2</sub>O(l), since these are the 'starting' species
All four species, including both Ag<sub>2</sub>O(s) and H<sub>2</sub>O(l), with equal weight
Only [HNO<sub>3</sub>] and [AgNO<sub>3</sub>], since Ag<sub>2</sub>O is a solid and H<sub>2</sub>O is the (near-constant, large-excess) solvent/pure liquid, both omitted by the same rule used for K
questions.explanation: Q uses exactly the same species-inclusion rule as K: pure solids (Ag<sub>2</sub>O) and, when acting as the solvent in large excess, pure liquids (H<sub>2</sub>O here) are omitted because their 'concentration' doesn't meaningfully change; only the aqueous, variable-concentration species (HNO<sub>3</sub> and AgNO<sub>3</sub>) enter Q — exactly mirroring how K would be written for this same reaction.
questions.hint: Whatever rule excludes species from K (pure solids, pure liquids in large excess) applies identically to Q, since Q and K share the same mathematical form.
distractor_logic: Q is defined by exactly the same expression-writing rules as K (just evaluated at non-equilibrium concentrations); it is never simply undefined just because a solid participates
Includes only the species that SHOULD be excluded, and excludes the ones that should actually be included
Wrongly includes species that a correctly written K for this same reaction would also have to exclude
mixed_topics: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constant

questions.question: The equilibrium vapour pressure of a pure liquid (a physical equilibrium, liquid ↔ vapour) is, in a sense, mathematically analogous to a K<sub>p</sub>-type equilibrium constant for a chemical reaction. What is the key similarity between the two?
options: Both are fixed at a given temperature and independent of how much liquid/solid or gas is present, as long as both phases coexist — just as K<sub>p</sub> for a chemical equilibrium doesn't depend on the starting amounts of reactants and products
Both depend on the volume of the container in exactly the same way
Both increase without limit as more substance is added, with no equilibrium ever being reached
There is no meaningful similarity; physical and chemical equilibria are governed by entirely unrelated mathematical rules
questions.explanation: Just as K<sub>p</sub> (or K<sub>c</sub>) for a chemical reaction depends only on temperature, not on the specific starting amounts of reactants and products, the equilibrium vapour pressure of a liquid depends only on temperature (for a given substance), not on how much liquid or vapour is actually present as long as both phases still coexist in the closed container — both are genuine equilibrium constants in the broader sense used throughout this chapter.
questions.hint: Recall the defining property of ANY equilibrium constant emphasised earlier in the chapter: what does it depend on, and what does it NOT depend on?
distractor_logic: Vapour pressure at equilibrium is a fixed value at a given temperature, independent of the container's volume as long as both liquid and vapour phases remain present (some vapour condenses or more liquid evaporates to maintain the same equilibrium pressure)
Both are bounded, equilibrium quantities — precisely because a genuine equilibrium is reached in each case, not runaway, ever-increasing behaviour

This is precisely the point of drawing the physical-equilibrium chapter section together with the chemical-equilibrium constant sections — the same core idea (a fixed, T-dependent equilibrium quantity) underlies both

questions.topic: Degree of Dissociation and Ostwald's Dilution Law
questions.question: A weak acid HA (K<sub>a</sub> = 1.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup>) at C = 0.1 M has degree of ionisation α ≈ √(K<sub>a</sub>/C). Its sodium salt NaA at the same 0.1 M concentration has degree of hydrolysis h ≈ √(K<sub>h</sub>/C), where K<sub>h</sub>=K<sub>w</sub>/K<sub>a</sub>. How do α and h compare in magnitude, and why?
options: h is larger than α, since salts are generally considered 'stronger' than their parent weak acids
Neither α nor h can be compared meaningfully, since one describes ionisation and the other hydrolysis, which are unrelated processes

α (≈ 0.01) is about 100 times larger than h (≈ 0.0001), because K<sub>a</sub> (1.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup>) is much larger than K<sub>h</sub> (1.0 × 10<sup>−9</sup>) — the acid itself ionises far more than its conjugate base hydrolyses
α and h are exactly equal, since both use the same √(constant/C) formula
questions.explanation: α = √(1.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup>/0.1) = √(1.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup>) = 0.01. K<sub>h</sub> = 1.0 × 10<sup>−14</sup>/1.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup> = 1.0 × 10<sup>−9</sup>, so h = √(1.0 × 10<sup>−9</sup>/0.1) = √(1.0 × 10<sup>−8</sup>) = 1.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup>. So α/h = 0.01/0.0001 = 100 — the acid ionises 100 times more than its salt hydrolyses, precisely because K<sub>a</sub> is 10,000 times larger than K<sub>h</sub>, and both quantities depend on the SQUARE ROOT of their respective constants, so a 10,000-fold ratio in the constants becomes only a 100-fold ratio (√10,000 = 100) in α versus h.
questions.hint: Compute both α and h using their respective formulas and constants, then compare — notice how the square-root relationship compresses a large ratio in K<sub>a</sub>/K<sub>h</sub> into a smaller ratio in α/h.
distractor_logic: Ionisation and hydrolysis are, mathematically, mirror-image equilibria connected by K<sub>a</sub>K<sub>b</sub>=K<sub>w</sub>-type relationships — 'stronger salt' isn't a meaningful basis for comparison here
Both processes are governed by essentially the same equilibrium mathematics (a √(constant/C) relationship), which is precisely what allows this direct, meaningful comparison
Assumes both ratios come out identical just because the same √(constant/C) formula is used, missing that K<sub>a</sub> and K<sub>h</sub> are very different numbers
mixed_topics: Degree of Dissociation and Ostwald's Dilution Law

questions.question: A saturated solution of AgCl is in contact with solid AgCl. If solid NaCl is now added directly to this mixture, describe the shift using Le Chatelier's principle and its effect on the amount of solid AgCl present.
options: The equilibrium shifts forward, dissolving more solid AgCl

The added Cl<sup>−</sup> is a common-ion 'concentration increase' stress; the AgCl dissolution equilibrium shifts backward (toward the solid), so the amount of solid AgCl actually INCREASES as some dissolved Ag<sup>+</sup> is pulled out of solution to combine with the excess Cl<sup>−</sup>
K<sub>sp</sub> of AgCl increases because more ions are now present in solution
Adding NaCl has no effect at all on this equilibrium, since NaCl is a different compound from AgCl
questions.explanation: Adding NaCl raises [Cl<sup>−</sup>], a genuine 'concentration increase' stress on the shared Cl<sup>−</sup> product of the AgCl(s) ↔ Ag<sup>+</sup> + Cl<sup>−</sup> equilibrium. By Le Chatelier's principle, the equilibrium shifts backward (toward the solid) to partially counteract this increase, meaning dissolved Ag<sup>+</sup> combines with some of the new Cl<sup>−</sup> to form more solid AgCl — so the amount of solid actually present increases, even as the total dissolved silver (molar solubility) decreases.
questions.hint: Distinguish two different things here: the DIRECTION of the shift (which way the reaction moves) versus the SOLUBILITY (how much stays dissolved) — the shift backward means MORE solid forms, i.e. less stays dissolved.
distractor_logic: Reverses the correct shift direction for an added common ion (a product-side species) — Le Chatelier predicts a shift AWAY from, not toward, the side with added stress
K<sub>sp</sub> is a genuine constant at fixed temperature — it does not increase just because more Cl<sup>−</sup> ions are added; what changes is the equilibrium POSITION, not K<sub>sp</sub> itself
NaCl supplies Cl<sup>−</sup>, which is directly a product species in AgCl's own dissolution equilibrium, making this a textbook common ion scenario, not an unrelated compound situation

questions.question: The ionic product of water, K<sub>w</sub>, increases as temperature rises (since water's self-ionisation, H<sub>2</sub>O ↔ H<sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>−</sup>, is endothermic). At 50°C, K<sub>w</sub> is larger than 1.0 × 10<sup>−14</sup>, so pure water's pH there is measurably LESS than 7. Is pure water at 50°C actually acidic?
options: Yes — any pH below 7 always means an acidic solution, by definition, regardless of temperature

No — it is still perfectly neutral, since [H<sup>+</sup>] still equals [OH<sup>−</sup>]; 'neutral' is defined by [H<sup>+</sup>]=[OH<sup>−</sup>], not by pH = 7 specifically (pH = 7 is only the neutral point AT 25°C)
The pH scale simply doesn't apply above 25°C, so the question is meaningless
Yes, because K<sub>w</sub> increasing with temperature is itself proof that water is becoming acidic
questions.explanation: Raising temperature shifts the endothermic self-ionisation of water forward (Le Chatelier's principle), increasing BOTH [H<sup>+</sup>] and [OH<sup>−</sup>] equally (they remain equal to each other, since water still produces them in a 1:1 ratio). This makes K<sub>w</sub> larger and pushes neutral pH below 7 — but the solution is still neutral, because neutrality is fundamentally defined by [H<sup>+</sup>] = [OH<sup>−</sup>], and pH = 7 is merely the numerical value this condition happens to correspond to specifically at 25°C.
questions.hint: Separate the DEFINITION of neutral (equal H<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>−</sup>) from the specific NUMBER '7', which is only tied to 25°C via K<sub>w</sub> = 10<sup>−14</sup> at that particular temperature.
distractor_logic: Wrongly treats 'pH = 7' as the universal, temperature-independent definition of neutral, rather than [H<sup>+</sup>] = [OH<sup>−</sup>] being the actual definition
The pH scale (based on [H<sup>+</sup>]) remains perfectly well defined at any temperature; only the specific numerical value corresponding to neutrality shifts with K<sub>w</sub>
Confuses the DIRECTION K<sub>w</sub> moves with a claim about acidity — increased self-ionisation increases both ions equally, which is neutral behaviour, not a shift toward acidity specifically
mixed_topics: Ionic Product of Water and the pH Scale

questions.question: K<sub>sp</sub> of PbCl<sub>2</sub> is 1.7 × 10<sup>−5</sup> (an AB<sub>2</sub>-type salt: PbCl<sub>2</sub> ↔ Pb<sup>2+</sup> + 2Cl<sup>−</sup>). Its molar solubility in pure water is ≈ 0.0162 M. What is its approximate molar solubility in a 0.1 M NaCl solution, and by roughly what factor is it reduced?
options: s ≈ 1.7 × 10<sup>−3</sup> M, a reduction by a factor of ≈ 9.5
s ≈ 1.7 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M, a reduction by a factor of ≈ 950
s ≈ 0.1 M, an increase, since more chloride should dissolve more lead chloride
s ≈ 0.0162 M, unchanged, since NaCl doesn't affect PbCl<sub>2</sub>'s equilibrium
questions.explanation: With [Cl<sup>−</sup>] ≈ 0.1 M fixed by the NaCl (an AB<sub>2</sub>-type common ion case, so the concentration must be SQUARED): K<sub>sp</sub> = s[Cl<sup>−</sup>]<sup>2</sup> ⇒ s = K<sub>sp</sub>/[Cl<sup>−</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = 1.7 × 10<sup>−5</sup>/(0.1)<sup>2</sup> = 1.7 × 10<sup>−3</sup> M. Compared to 0.0162 M in pure water, this is a reduction by a factor of ≈0.0162/0.0017 ≈ 9.5.
questions.hint: Remember to square [Cl<sup>−</sup>] in the denominator, since PbCl<sub>2</sub> is an AB<sub>2</sub>-type salt — a very common place to under-count the exponent in a common-ion solubility problem.
distractor_logic: Forgets to square [Cl<sup>−</sup>], treating this like a simple AB-type common ion problem instead of the correct AB<sub>2</sub> treatment, giving a much smaller apparent reduction
Reverses the entire direction of the common ion effect — adding a common ion always suppresses, never enhances, the solubility of a sparingly soluble salt
Ignores the common ion's suppressing effect on solubility entirely

questions.topic: Acids, Bases and the Lewis Concept
questions.question: Using the Bronsted-Lowry concept, explain the hydrolysis reaction CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O ↔ CH<sub>3</sub>COOH + OH<sup>−</sup> in terms of which species acts as the acid and which as the base.
options: OH<sup>−</sup> is the acid in this reaction, since hydroxide ions are normally associated with basic behaviour
Neither species undergoes any proton transfer; this is a purely physical dissolution process
CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> acts as the acid, donating a proton to H<sub>2</sub>O

H<sub>2</sub>O acts as the Bronsted-Lowry acid (donating a proton to CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>, which acts as the base, accepting it to become CH<sub>3</sub>COOH), leaving OH<sup>−</sup> behind as the conjugate base of water
questions.explanation: Tracking the proton: H<sub>2</sub>O loses one H (becoming OH<sup>−</sup>), so water is the proton DONOR, i.e. the Bronsted-Lowry acid in this specific reaction; CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> gains that proton (becoming CH<sub>3</sub>COOH), acting as the base. This is exactly why CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>, as the conjugate base of a weak acid, is basic enough to hydrolyse water at all, producing the OH<sup>−</sup> responsible for sodium acetate solutions being basic.
questions.hint: Track which species ends up with one more H atom compared to the left-hand side of the equation — that species was the proton acceptor (base).
distractor_logic: OH<sup>−</sup> here is a PRODUCT of the reaction (the conjugate base of water, formed once water donates its proton), not itself acting as an acid in this particular step
This is very much a genuine proton-transfer (Bronsted-Lowry acid-base) reaction, not merely a physical process — it's the same kind of equilibrium as ordinary weak acid/base ionisation
Reverses the acid/base roles — CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> gains, rather than donates, a proton in this specific reaction
mixed_topics: Acids, Bases and the Lewis Concept

questions.topic: Ionization of Weak Acids and Bases
questions.question: A buffer contains 0.3 M CH<sub>3</sub>COONa and 0.2 M CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, where K<sub>a</sub> of acetic acid = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup> is given directly (not as pK<sub>a</sub>). What is the pH of this buffer?
options: ≈ 4.57
≈ 5.09
≈ 4.92
≈ 4.74
questions.explanation: First, pK<sub>a</sub> = −log(1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>) ≈ 4.74. Then pH = pK<sub>a</sub> + log([salt]/[acid]) = 4.74 + log(0.3/0.2) = 4.74 + log(1.5) ≈ 4.74 + 0.176 ≈ 4.92.
questions.hint: Convert the given K<sub>a</sub> to pK<sub>a</sub> first (Ionization topic), then apply the buffer formula with the actual 0.3:0.2 ratio (not assuming it's 1:1).
distractor_logic: Undershoots the correction, applying too small a log adjustment for the given 0.3:0.2 ratio
Miscalculates the log(1.5) correction with the wrong sign/magnitude, overshooting the true pH
Uses pK<sub>a</sub> alone, forgetting to add the log(1.5) correction for the actual, non-equal salt/acid ratio given
