topics.name: Dynamic Equilibrium and Physical Equilibria
topics.summary: Equilibrium can occur in purely physical changes, not just chemical reactions. In a closed container, a solid melts and freezes at equal rates (solid ↔ liquid), a liquid evaporates and condenses at equal rates (liquid ↔ vapour, giving a fixed vapour pressure at each temperature), and a solute dissolves and re-deposits at equal rates once a solution is saturated. The defining feature is that it must be a closed system: if vapour or dissolved gas can escape, the opposing process never catches up, and true equilibrium is never reached — the substance simply runs out or the system changes one-way. At equilibrium, measurable properties (vapour pressure, amount of undissolved solid, ice-water ratio) become constant with time, even though molecules keep moving between phases — this is dynamic, not static, equilibrium. All the mathematics used later for chemical equilibrium constants (K depends only on temperature, not on amounts present) applies equally to these physical equilibria.
key_formulas: Equilibrium requires: rate(forward process) = rate(reverse process)
Vapour pressure is fixed at a given T for a closed liquid↔vapour system
topics.worked_example: Water sealed in a stoppered flask at 25°C: evaporation and condensation rates become equal once the vapour pressure reaches 23.8 mm Hg; this value stays fixed regardless of how much liquid water remains, as long as some liquid is still present.
common_mistakes: Treating an OPEN container (where vapour escapes) as if it reaches the same equilibrium as a closed one
Believing equilibrium means the forward or reverse process has stopped, rather than both continuing at equal rates
Assuming a physical equilibrium constant (like vapour pressure) depends on how much substance is present

topics.name: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constant
topics.summary: The law of chemical equilibrium (law of mass action) states that for aA + bB ↔ cC + dD at a given temperature, the ratio Kc = [C]c[D]d/([A]a[B]b) (products over reactants, each concentration raised to its stoichiometric coefficient) is constant at equilibrium, regardless of the starting concentrations. Kc depends ONLY on temperature: it doesn't change with the initial amounts taken, with pressure/volume changes, or with a catalyst (a catalyst speeds up how fast equilibrium is reached, never where it ends up). The MAGNITUDE of K tells you about the equilibrium position: K >> 1 means mostly products at equilibrium; K << 1 means mostly reactants; K near 1 means comparable amounts of both. Reversing a reaction inverts K (Kreverse = 1/Kforward), and combining two equilibria by addition multiplies their K values.
key_formulas: For A↔B (K<sub>1</sub>) then B↔C (K<sub>2</sub>): K(A↔C) = K<sub>1</sub> × K<sub>2</sub>
topics.worked_example: For H<sub>2</sub>(g)+I<sub>2</sub>(g)↔2HI(g), if 0.30 mol each of H<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>2</sub> react from initial 0.40 mol L<sup>−1</sup> each in a 1 L flask, equilibrium concentrations are [H<sub>2</sub>]=[I<sub>2</sub>]=0.10 M, [HI]=0.60 M, giving K<sub>c</sub>=(0.60)<sup>2</sup>/(0.10×0.10)=36.
common_mistakes: Believing K<sub>c</sub> changes with the initial concentrations used (only the equilibrium POSITION changes; K itself doesn't)
Believing a catalyst changes the value of K
Forgetting to raise each concentration to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient

topics.name: Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Equilibria
topics.summary: An equilibrium is homogeneous when every reactant and product is in the same phase (usually all gases, like N2(g)+3H2(g)↔2NH3(g), or all in one solution). It is heterogeneous when species exist in more than one phase (a solid or pure liquid mixed with gases or solutions), such as CaCO3(s)↔CaO(s)+CO2(g). The key rule for heterogeneous equilibria: pure solids and pure liquids are OMITTED from the equilibrium expression, because their molar concentration (density ÷ molar mass) is an intrinsic, constant property that doesn't change as the reaction proceeds — it is absorbed into the value of K itself. Only species whose concentration can actually vary (gases, dissolved solutes) appear in Kc or Kp. This also means changing the AMOUNT of a pure solid/liquid present (as long as some remains) has zero effect on the equilibrium position, since it never appeared in the expression to begin with.
topics.worked_example: For Ni(s)+4CO(g)↔Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>(g) with [CO]=0.50 M and [Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>]=0.020 M at equilibrium: K<sub>c</sub>=0.020/(0.50)<sup>4</sup>=0.020/0.0625=0.32 (Ni(s) is left out entirely).
common_mistakes: Including a pure solid or pure liquid's 'concentration' in the K expression
Assuming adding more solid reactant shifts a heterogeneous equilibrium, when it has no effect at all
Forgetting to raise a gas-phase species to its correct stoichiometric power in a heterogeneous expression

topics.name: Reaction Quotient and Predicting Direction
topics.summary: The reaction quotient Q has exactly the same mathematical form as K, but can be evaluated at ANY point during a reaction, not just at equilibrium — it's a snapshot using whatever concentrations exist at that instant. Comparing Q to K tells you which way the reaction will shift to reach equilibrium: if Q < K, there's proportionally too little product, so the forward reaction proceeds; if Q > K, there's too much product, so the reverse reaction proceeds; if Q = K, the system is already at equilibrium. This comparison is the quantitative engine behind Le Chatelier's principle: any 'stress' (adding reactant, removing product, changing volume) instantly changes Q away from K, and the reaction then runs in whichever direction brings Q back to K. Qp is the pressure-based analogue, compared against Kp the same way.
key_formulas: Q<sub>c</sub> = [C]<sup>c</sup>[D]<sup>d</sup> / [A]<sup>a</sup>[B]<sup>b</sup> (at any instant, same form as K<sub>c</sub>)
Q < K → forward shift; Q > K → reverse shift; Q = K → at equilibrium
topics.worked_example: For H<sub>2</sub>+I<sub>2</sub>↔2HI, K<sub>c</sub>=50. At an instant with [H<sub>2</sub>]=[I<sub>2</sub>]=0.50 M and [HI]=4.0 M: Q<sub>c</sub>=(4.0)<sup>2</sup>/(0.50×0.50)=64 > 50, so the reaction proceeds in reverse.
common_mistakes: Computing Q correctly but then reversing the Q-vs-K directional conclusion
Forgetting to square or cube concentrations according to stoichiometry when computing Q
Comparing a pressure-based Q<sub>p</sub> against a concentration-based K<sub>c</sub> (or vice versa) without converting first

topics.name: Relationship Between K<sub>p</sub> and K<sub>c</sub>
topics.summary: For gas-phase equilibria, K can be expressed either in terms of concentrations (K<sub>c</sub>) or partial pressures (K<sub>p</sub>). They are related by K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub>(RT)<sup>Δn</sup>, where Δn = (moles of gaseous products) − (moles of gaseous reactants) from the balanced equation, R is the gas constant, and T is absolute temperature. If Δn = 0 (equal gas moles on both sides), K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub> exactly, since (RT)<sup>0</sup> = 1. If Δn is positive, K<sub>p</sub> > K<sub>c</sub> (assuming RT > 1); if negative, K<sub>p</sub> < K<sub>c</sub>. This conversion is purely a units/bookkeeping relationship between two ways of describing the SAME equilibrium at the SAME temperature — it does not mean K<sub>p</sub> and K<sub>c</sub> respond differently to temperature changes; both still change together as dictated by Le Chatelier's principle when T actually changes.
key_formulas: Δn = (gas moles of products) − (gas moles of reactants)
common_mistakes: Using the wrong sign of Δn (multiplying by (RT) when dividing was needed, or vice versa)
Forgetting to include Δn as an exponent, effectively treating (RT)<sup>Δn</sup> as just (RT) regardless of the actual stoichiometry
Assuming K<sub>p</sub>=K<sub>c</sub> always, rather than only when Δn=0

topics.name: Le Chatelier's Principle
topics.summary: Le Chatelier's principle: when a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure/volume, or temperature, it shifts in the direction that partially counteracts that change. Increasing a reactant's (or decreasing a product's) concentration shifts equilibrium forward, and vice versa. Increasing pressure (decreasing volume) shifts equilibrium toward the side with FEWER moles of gas; decreasing pressure favours the side with MORE gas moles; if both sides have equal gas moles, pressure has no effect. For temperature, heat acts like a 'reactant' in an endothermic reaction and like a 'product' in an exothermic one: raising T always shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction (increasing K for that direction), and lowering T shifts it in the exothermic direction. Two important exceptions: a catalyst speeds up both forward and reverse rates equally, reaching equilibrium faster WITHOUT shifting its position or changing K; and adding an inert gas at constant volume doesn't change any reacting species' partial pressure/concentration, so it causes no shift (at constant pressure, however, inert gas addition increases volume and does shift equilibrium toward more gas moles).
key_formulas: High pressure → shifts toward fewer gas moles
Exothermic reaction: higher T → K decreases (shifts reverse)
Endothermic reaction: higher T → K increases (shifts forward)
topics.worked_example: For N<sub>2</sub>(g)+3H<sub>2</sub>(g)↔2NH<sub>3</sub>(g) (exothermic, 4 mol gas → 2 mol gas): low temperature AND high pressure both favour maximum NH<sub>3</sub> yield, since they act in the same helpful direction.
common_mistakes: Believing a catalyst shifts equilibrium position or changes K (it only speeds up reaching the same equilibrium)
Reversing which temperature direction favours an exothermic vs endothermic reaction
Assuming inert gas addition always shifts equilibrium, without checking whether volume is held constant or pressure is held constant

topics.name: Acids, Bases and the Lewis Concept
topics.summary: Three acid-base concepts build on each other in generality. The Arrhenius concept (most limited) defines an acid as a substance that gives H+ in water and a base as one giving OH−. The Bronsted-Lowry concept is broader: an acid is any proton (H+) DONOR, a base is any proton ACCEPTOR, regardless of solvent. Every Bronsted acid/base reaction produces a conjugate pair differing by exactly one proton (e.g. NH3/NH4+). Some species (like HCO3−) are amphoteric, able to act as either acid or base depending on what they react with. The Lewis concept is the most general: an acid is an electron-pair ACCEPTOR, a base is an electron-pair DONOR, extending acid-base behaviour to reactions with no protons at all (e.g. BF3, a Lewis acid, accepting a lone pair from NH3, a Lewis base). A Lewis-acid-specific reaction has no meaningful Ka in the Bronsted sense, since Ka describes proton-transfer ionisation.
key_formulas: Bronsted acid: proton donor; Bronsted base: proton acceptor
Lewis acid: electron-pair acceptor; Lewis base: electron-pair donor
topics.worked_example: NH<sub>3</sub>+H<sub>2</sub>O↔NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>+OH<sup>−</sup>: conjugate pairs are NH<sub>3</sub>/NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> and H<sub>2</sub>O/OH<sup>−</sup>; here water acts as the Bronsted acid.
common_mistakes: Mixing up the Bronsted-Lowry and Lewis definitions of acid and base
Failing to correctly identify conjugate pairs (they must differ by exactly one proton)
Assuming a species can only ever be an acid OR a base, missing amphoteric behaviour

topics.name: Ionization of Weak Acids and Bases
topics.summary: For a weak acid HA ↔ H+ + A−, the ionization constant Ka = [H+][A−]/[HA] measures the extent of ionisation: larger Ka means a stronger (more ionised) acid. Similarly, a weak base has Kb. pKa = −log Ka (and pKb similarly) gives more convenient numbers; SMALLER pKa means a STRONGER acid. For any conjugate acid-base pair, Ka × Kb = Kw — a strong-ish acid always has a very weak conjugate base, and vice versa. For polyprotic (diprotic, triprotic) acids, ionisation happens in successive steps with Ka1 >> Ka2 >> Ka3 (each proton is harder to remove from an increasingly negative species); [H+] is set almost entirely by the first step, and the final anion's concentration often reduces neatly to just Ka2 (or the last step's constant) once the first-step [H+]≈[intermediate anion] terms cancel.
topics.worked_example: Acetic acid K<sub>a</sub>=1.8×10<sup>−5</sup> gives pK<sub>a</sub>≈4.74; its conjugate base's K<sub>b</sub>(CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>)=K<sub>w</sub>/K<sub>a</sub>≈5.6×10<sup>−10</sup>.
common_mistakes: Confusing K<sub>a</sub> and pK<sub>a</sub> (a LARGER K<sub>a</sub> but SMALLER pK<sub>a</sub> both mean a stronger acid)
Adding K<sub>a</sub> and K<sub>b</sub> instead of multiplying them to relate a conjugate pair
Treating both ionisation steps of a diprotic acid as equally significant, instead of recognising K<sub>a1</sub> dominates [H<sup>+</sup>]

topics.name: Ionic Product of Water and the pH Scale
topics.summary: Water self-ionises very slightly: H<sub>2</sub>O ↔ H<sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>−</sup>, with ionic product K<sub>w</sub> = [H<sup>+</sup>][OH<sup>−</sup>] = 1.0 × 10<sup>−14</sup> at 25°C. pH = −log[H<sup>+</sup>] and pOH = −log[OH<sup>−</sup>], with pH + pOH = 14 at 25°C (since K<sub>w</sub> is fixed at that temperature). Neutral means [H<sup>+</sup>]=[OH<sup>−</sup>] (pH=7 at 25°C specifically); acidic means pH<7; basic means pH>7 — but these numeric cutoffs shift at other temperatures since K<sub>w</sub> itself changes (self-ionisation is endothermic, so K<sub>w</sub> rises with temperature, and 'neutral' pH drops below 7 at higher T while STILL being genuinely neutral). For strong acids/bases, [H<sup>+</sup>] or [OH<sup>−</sup>] equals the given concentration directly (times any ionisable-proton/hydroxide count, e.g. ×2 for Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub>). Mixing solutions requires averaging actual ion CONCENTRATIONS (weighted by volume), never averaging pH values directly.
topics.worked_example: 0.005 M Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> gives [OH<sup>−</sup>]=2×0.005=0.01 M, pOH=2, so pH=14−2=12.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the factor of 2 (or more) for polyprotic bases/acids like Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> or H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> before taking the log
Averaging two pH values directly when mixing solutions, instead of averaging the underlying [H<sup>+</sup>] concentrations
Assuming pH=7 always means neutral, regardless of temperature

topics.name: Degree of Dissociation and Ostwald's Dilution Law
topics.summary: The degree of dissociation α is the fraction (0 to 1) of a weak electrolyte that has ionised at equilibrium. Ostwald's dilution law gives the approximate relation α ≈ √(Ka/C) for small α (derived by assuming 1−α ≈ 1 in the full expression Ka = Cα2/(1−α)); this shows α INCREASES on dilution (as C decreases), approaching 1 at infinite dilution — the ratio form α1/α2 = √(C2/C1) is convenient for comparing two concentrations directly. When α is NOT small (high concentration relative to Ka, or Ka itself large), the simple square-root approximation becomes inaccurate and the FULL quadratic Cα2+Kaα−Ka=0 must be solved instead. Once α is known, [H+] = Cα (not α alone) gives the actual ion concentration needed for pH calculations.
topics.worked_example: 0.1 M CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, K<sub>a</sub>=1.8×10<sup>−5</sup>: α≈√(1.8×10<sup>−4</sup>)≈0.0134 (1.34%); diluting to 0.01 M raises α to ≈0.042 (4.2%).
common_mistakes: Stopping at α itself when the question actually asks for [H<sup>+</sup>] (=Cα), a very easy final step to skip
Using the small-α approximation when α is actually large (high C<sub>0</sub> relative to K<sub>a</sub>), requiring the full quadratic instead
Getting the dilution trend backwards (α increases, not decreases, on dilution)

topics.name: Common Ion Effect
topics.summary: The common ion effect: adding an ion that is ALREADY a product of a given equilibrium suppresses that equilibrium, shifting it backward (by Le Chatelier's principle). For a weak acid HA, adding a salt of its conjugate base (like NaA) supplies extra A−, pushing HA↔H++A− backward and lowering both α and [H+] — approximated as [H+] ≈ Ka[acid]/[salt] once the common ion dominates. The same logic applies to a weak base with a common cation, or to a sparingly soluble salt: adding a common ion to a saturated solution (e.g. NaCl added to a saturated AgCl solution) suppresses further dissolution, LOWERING molar solubility (s = Ksp/[common ion], or divided by [common ion]2 for an AB2-type salt). The effect can be dramatic: even a modest common-ion concentration can suppress solubility or ionisation by several orders of magnitude.
key_formulas: s ≈ K<sub>sp</sub>/[common ion] (AB-type salt + common ion)
topics.worked_example: AgCl (K<sub>sp</sub>=1.8×10<sup>−10</sup>) has s≈1.34×10<sup>−5</sup> M in pure water, but only s≈1.8×10<sup>−9</sup> M in 0.1 M NaCl — roughly a 7,450-fold reduction.
common_mistakes: Getting the direction backwards (a common ion SUPPRESSES, never promotes, further ionisation/dissolution)
Forgetting to square the common ion's concentration for an AB<sub>2</sub>-type salt when applying the common-ion solubility shortcut
Applying the common ion effect to an ion that isn't actually shared with the specific equilibrium in question

topics.name: Hydrolysis of Salts
topics.summary: When a salt dissolves, its ions can react with water (hydrolysis) if they are the conjugate acid/base of a WEAK parent acid/base. A salt of a weak acid + strong base (e.g. CH3COONa) hydrolyses to give a BASIC solution (pH = 7 + ½pKa + ½log C). A salt of a weak base + strong acid (e.g. NH4Cl) hydrolyses to give an ACIDIC solution (pH = 7 − ½pKb − ½log C). A salt of a weak acid + weak base gives pH ≈ 7 + ½pKa − ½pKb, which is close to neutral only when pKa≈pKb; otherwise it shifts toward whichever parent is comparatively stronger (smaller pK). A salt of a strong acid + strong base (like NaCl) doesn't hydrolyse at all and gives a neutral solution. The hydrolysis constant Kh = Kw/Ka (or Kw/Kb) and degree of hydrolysis h ≈ √(Kh/C) follow the exact same mathematical pattern as Ostwald's dilution law for ordinary weak-acid ionisation.
common_mistakes: Mixing up which salt-type formula (weak-acid-salt vs weak-base-salt) applies, giving the wrong acidic/basic character
Assuming all salts of a weak acid and weak base are automatically neutral, ignoring unequal pK<sub>a</sub>/pK<sub>b</sub> values
Confusing a lightly-hydrolysed salt solution with a genuine buffer (a salt alone lacks enough of the conjugate species to resist real pH stress)

topics.name: Buffer Solutions
topics.summary: A buffer solution resists significant pH change when small amounts of acid or base are added, or upon dilution. An acidic buffer is a mixture of a weak acid and a salt of its conjugate base (e.g. CH3COOH/CH3COONa) in comparable amounts; a basic buffer pairs a weak base with a salt of its conjugate acid (e.g. NH4OH/NH4Cl). The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]) (or pOH = pKb + log([salt]/[base]), then pH = 14−pOH), gives the buffer's pH directly from the salt-to-acid (or salt-to-base) ratio. When that ratio is exactly 1, pH = pKa exactly. Because pH depends only on the RATIO of the two concentrations, diluting a buffer changes both concentrations by the same factor, leaving the ratio (and hence pH) almost unchanged — the key reason buffers resist both added acid/base AND dilution so much better than an unbuffered solution.
key_formulas: Equal salt and acid concentrations ⇒ pH = pK<sub>a</sub>
common_mistakes: Assuming buffer pH always equals pK<sub>a</sub>, forgetting the log(ratio) correction when salt and acid concentrations actually differ
Getting the sign of the ratio backwards (using [acid]/[salt] instead of [salt]/[acid])
Forgetting the final pH = 14 − pOH conversion step for a BASIC buffer

topics.name: Solubility Product (K<sub>sp</sub>)
topics.summary: For a sparingly soluble salt AxBy(s) ↔ xAy+ + yBx−, the solubility product Ksp = [Ay+]x[Bx−]y (the solid is omitted, as with any pure solid). Relating Ksp to molar solubility s depends entirely on the salt's ion ratio: for an AB-type salt (like AgCl), Ksp=s2; for an AB2 or A2B-type salt (like CaF2 or Ag2CrO4), Ksp=4s3 (don't forget to SQUARE the stoichiometric factor of 2 along with s). Comparing the actual ionic product Qsp to Ksp predicts behaviour exactly like Q versus K elsewhere: Qsp > Ksp means precipitation occurs (mixing two solutions often creates this condition, since concentrations are diluted upon mixing but the product can still exceed Ksp); Qsp < Ksp means the solution is unsaturated with no precipitate. The common ion effect and differing Ksp/threshold values between salts also enable SELECTIVE precipitation, separating ions by adding a shared precipitating agent gradually.
key_formulas: Q<sub>sp</sub> > K<sub>sp</sub> → precipitation; Q<sub>sp</sub> < K<sub>sp</sub> → no precipitation
common_mistakes: Using the AB-type square-root formula for an AB<sub>2</sub>-type salt (or vice versa), ignoring the actual ion ratio
Forgetting to halve concentrations (dilution) when computing Q<sub>sp</sub> after mixing two solutions of equal volume
Forgetting to square the stoichiometric coefficient of the more-abundant ion in the 4s<sup>3</sup>-type formula
